Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. At the close of the impressive ceremony of "La nuit des lies" sponsored by the city of Montreal on the evening of June 30, 1964, to mark the taking over of St. Helen's island and the island of Notre Dame by the World Exhibition Corporation, the band played England's royal anthem, to the obvious displeasure of most spectators because only the national anthem "O Canada" appeared on the program.
In view of the fact that this awe-inspiring event was bound to have world-wide repercussions the time was very ill chosen to show that Canada is still a subject country. Under those circumstances when every trace of the red ensign had been removed from St. Helen's island, I feel that the playing of the English royal anthem was a truly provocative action. Whoever took that step had no right to do so, and I wish to protest most emphatically against such a gesture of colonialism.

Mr. Speaker, the situation in Cyprus is certainly not free from serious concern. The secretary general of the United Nations was in touch this morning with our representative at the United Nations. I was in touch with the secretary general before Sunday last, following the talks I had with the prime minister of Greece and the prime minister of Turkey. The secretary general of NATO is in Ottawa today and we are glad to have the opportunity of discussing this matter with him, particularly in view of his visit on June 4 to the governments of Greece and Turkey.
I cannot say whether the press reports mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition are exactly in accordance with the facts. There are reasons for believing, however, that there have been importations of one kind or another. Beyond that I do not want to go at this time.

However, I will say that the introduction of regular army units by one or both sides involved in the Cyprus dispute would be contrary to the security council resolution of March 4, which calls upon all member states to refrain from any action likely to worsen the situation. It would be contrary also to the obligations undertaken by all members of NATO. If such regular forces from the mainland were introduced on Cyprus 20220-313
Inquiries of the Ministry a new and dangerous situation would be created for the United Nations peace keeping force, as it has neither the mandate nor the strength to interpose itself between large, well equipped forces if hostilities should break out. Indeed, the force was not established for that purpose.
In my discussions with Prime Minister Inonu and Prime Minister Papandreou last week I stressed our concern over the possibility of such a development. I stressed the responsibilities of both Greece and Turkey to abide by their obligations to the United Nations and to NATO.
Our mission to the United Nations in New York has been instructed, as I have already indicated, to keep in close and continuous contract with the United Nations secretariat in order to make known our concern about the position of the Canadian contingent in the peace keeping force, because of the possibility that additional troops are being landed on Cyprus from the mainland. The Canadian forces participating in the United Nations peace keeping operation are under the command of the United Nations commander pursuant to the security council resolution of March 4. Any action taken by Canada will be as a member of the United Nations force.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 30, consideration of the motion by Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves joined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

Mr. Speaker, at 10.30 p.m. on Tuesday I had suggested to the house a formula for the selection of a flag by means of a plebiscite, giving to the people five distinct choices. I contended that by this formula the final choice would be the design that received the largest number of votes. That is the preferential system. I also suggested that by using this method no hint of partisanship would remain like a dry and bitter ash once the fires engendered by this debate had died away.
In the remaining time left to me I wish to comment on a letter sent by special delivery mail and addressed to the Prime Minister, from 12 distinguished Canadians of varying academic disciplines and the professions. I suggest their views have been dismissed out of hand by the Prime Minister as being of no consequence. Their position, however, has been endorsed by the editor of the Canadian Commentator and also by several other academics and people of good will.
I suggest that the core of the trouble with the way the Prime Minister has attemped to foist his flag upon us is that little or no attention has been paid to the thoughtful efforts of interested Canadians to remind the government of the traditions which should be embodied in any design for a flag. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that rather than engendering in Canada any fervent feeling of patriotism and pride, the new flag will only produce a yawn of indifference.
Patrick Duncan, in writing of Jan Christian Smuts, the last statesman of South Africa, said something which I think might be applied with remarkable exactitude to the Prime Minister. He said:
I only wish I thought that his fine sentiments were more intimately hitched on to the springs which govern his actions. They do sometimes get turned on, but they spend much of their time in the cupboard of his soul.

The cupboard of the Prime Minister's soul has been a crowded and confused place of late as he repudiates those traditions of scholarship which were his first vocation.
I want to be very frank, Mr. Speaker. I am not at all convinced, or have not been convinced as yet by any argument I have heard, that the new flag will be a source of national unity; and if it is not that it is nothing. I am not all convinced that by tearing up the past we will in fact be adopting any formula which will bring inspiration to most Canadians in the future.
Most of the letters which have been sent to me by hundreds of my constituents are very reasonable about the flag. These letters show a remarkable desire for compromise, in that they indicate support for any flag which would include symbols representative of the best traditions of both the founding races. Obviously in my part of Canada these symbols would include the union jack, but are we about to turn our backs on this evidence of good will and select a flag which is neither a source of national unity nor unmistakably Canadian in character? Are the people I represent to be deprived of all their traditions and find a substitute is not even acceptable to their partners in other parts of Canada?
The letter to the Prime Minister puts it this way:
The very essence of this country's history, and the reason for our national distinctiveness, has been the long and often turbulent marriage of French and English heritages. We have faith that in their depths Canadians pride themselves on this *union, and on its parliamentary and non-revolutionary tradition. Canada has a continuous history of 350 years of French speaking and English speaking life together in North America, and 200 years of union. The creative tension between the two founding peoples has been a guarantee to other racial groups of their continued identity, in contrast to the American concept of the melting pot. These are the positive facts of our history; we cannot change them; they give Canada its sinews. The nation is strong enough to face its own past proudly, and to assert it. Whatever may be said about the use of the maple leaf as a Canadian emblem in the past, it has never gained anyone's vigorous allegiance, and it involves no commitment to the human fact of Canada.
We believe that Canada has a distinguished culture of its own. We believe that this is a positive culture. We believe that the basis of this positive culture is a frank acceptance of both the English Canadian and French Canadian civilizations. We believe that a distinctive Canadian flag should reflect this positive fact.
It is not enough, I suggest, to use a flag to get rid of something, to repudiate the task or to deny the facts of history. We in Canada are becoming a nation of jellyfish, to use an expression of the late Dr. Sidney Smith. In 20220-314
Canadian Flag
an interesting speech at the University of New Brunswick in 1962 Dr. Frank Underhill recalled the suggestion made in 1865 by Henri Joly de Lotbiniere, who proposed the adoption of the rainbow as our emblem. Dr. Underhill said that he himself "sometimes played with the idea of submitting his own design for a national flag to the authorities. It would consist of a green maple leaf in the centre, surrounded by Joly's multicoloured rainbows, the whole upon a background of pure white to signify our Canadian innocence of colonialism, imperialism, unitarianism, Americanism, capitalism, socialism and all the other 20th century sins."
The design proposed in the resolution before us, Mr. Speaker, is neither positive nor affirmative. It is an artificial attempt to honour an election promise hastily made. It is devious in that a palliative or sop is being offered in an obscure way by means of a second resolution to those whose views on flags can never be reconciled to the otherwise acceptable position taken on various aspects of policy by the government. Perhaps in the short run the new flag will find acceptance in Quebec but I predict that before too many years have passed it will be ridiculed and turned aside because of its utter failure to incorporate anything of the French heritage in its design. Pierre Elliot Trudeau is quoted in the Toronto Star of June 12 of this year as having said:
Quebec doesn't give a tinker's damn about the new flag. The flag is a matter of complete indifference in Quebec.
The Prime Minister must bear the heavy responsibility of forcing the flag to become a contentious party issue. His sense of timing, I suggest, is little less than appalling. His sense of history is non-existent. His sense of magnanimity is totally absent. So, Mr. Speaker, both the founding races are going to be the ultimate losers if this new traditionless and septic flag is adopted, a flag proposed by a minority government because the latest techniques of opinion making falteringly urge it on.
What a sordid place this parliament has become. How denuded of any sense of relevancy. We who are asked by the vast majority of our constituents to stand by and honour our heritage are derided as somehow being against Canada itself.
I wish to end by recalling again the appeal to realism in politics by the group of seven young French Canadian intellectuals who are able to understand a concept beyond the

Canadian Flag
narrow provincialism which is so much and so unfortunately a part of our land. They say:
The most valid trends today are toward more enlightened humanism, toward various forms of political, social and economic universalism. Canada is a reproduction on a smaller and simpler scale of this universal phenomenon. The challenge is for a number of ethnic groups to learn to live together. It is a modem challenge, meaningful and indicative of what can be expected from man. If Canadians cannot make a success of a country such as theirs, how can they contribute in any way to the elaboration of humanism, to the formulation of the international political structures of tomorrow? To confess one's inability to make Canadian confederation work is, at this stage of history, to admit one's unworthiness to contribute to the universal order.

May I ask my hon. friend a question with regard to the earlier part of his remarks on Tuesday? I was very interested in his proposal to have five questions on a referendum. I wanted to ask my hon. friend if he would envisage the use of some kind of preferential voting system whereby one would knock off the least popular, the one that received the fewest first choices, then give the second choices to the others and gradually in that way build up to the one most popular choice.

If my hon. friend had been gripped as she should have been by my first remarks this afternoon she would have noticed that I used the phrase "preferential system". That is what I implied in my suggestion.
May I ask one more question?
Not an argument.

No, just a question. I am really interested in knowing what the hon. member would do if some people only put down one choice. As my hon. friend knows, the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia used a preferential voting system, and that was why they abandoned it. People tend to plump for one thing. They only give one preference, with the result that you might get 20 per cent, 15, 15, and 20, with no majority at all. What would my hon. friend do in that case? How would he get them to put down their choices?

I cannot presume to speak for the people of Canada on how they would vote or not vote on what to me is a reasonably simple selection of five alternative choices. If people want to use the system known in New Brunswick as the plumper I have no real criticism of that system.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph P. O'Keefe (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been a Canadian for just over 15 years, and my feeling is that too much has been made in Canada of issues that tend to divide when the emphasis should be on the things all Canadians have in common, the things that should help, even impel, us to unite. If I did not believe with all my mind that a truly Canadian flag would help to unite all Canadians, particularly all future Canadians, I could not in conscience support this resolution. We must look at this flag not only with our eyes but with our intelligence and our imagination.
I feel that new Canadians in Newfoundland see this flag situation in a better perspective than may be available to others; and these new Canadians, nearly 80,000 of whom are my constituents, are asking this question and are waiting for an intelligent and satisfactory answer. Should the flag be an issue? I think it should, even although this government's decision and solution may be regarded by some as a political compromise. Even if that view is correct, what is wrong with this kind of a solution? It has been tried successfully all through history.
A distinctive flag is adopted for the purpose of international recognition. I am confident that it will, in time, become a truly national symbol. There is a good argument in favour of this resolution which those who prefer the red ensign and the union jack may acknowledge, since they are not denied the right to fly a flag of their own sentimental preference. On May 20 I signed a telegram addressed to my Newfoundland constituents which read:
I am prepared to support a national flag which cannot be mistaken for the emblem of any other country, provided official recognition is also given to the union jack as a symbol of Canada's membership in the commonwealth and of our loyalty to the crown.
I believe, with all the sincerity of which I am capable, that now is the time for Canadians to fly a flag that is truly distinctive; a flag easily recognizable as Canada's own, easily identifiable; a flag that cannot be mistaken for the symbol of any other country; a flag for our Canadian future which recognizes and honours the past; a flag that has little new but contains all the best of the old. This, I believe, the new flag does.
May I emphasize that when I made my decision on this matter it was not necessarily my own, personal preference. I attempted to make a choice, not for myself, indeed not just for my constituents in Newfoundland but, as a member of parliament should, for the whole of Canada. I have always accepted and indeed,

as a Newfoundlander, supported the union jack and, as a Canadian, the red ensign. But when there was, as there is, presented to parliament a flag which I believe to be more representative of Canada and Canadians as a whole, especially when looking into the future, then I gave, and I am giving my support to the adoption of this flag.
I happen to be a Roman Catholic of Irish descent. Despite the quietening effect of the passing years, memories of old world strifes, of wrongs and of bitter oppression are not easily forgotten. We still read history. There are those of us who remember. My Irish forebears gave up most of their possessions to live in rugged Newfoundland, where living has never been easy. In many cases, even here oppression and bigotry followed them. Where indeed, a little more than 100 years ago it was a crime to even live. Great and heroic men took part in the early colonization of my island, and the glory which their names shed on its history should never be forgotten. A knowledge of the changes, the struggles and the suffering through which my people of Newfoundland passed can never fail to be one of deep and abiding interest.
It may be of some interest to our Quebec friends to know that there was a time when Newfoundland actually helped to save not just Quebec but Canada. It was late in the eighteenth century, when in a moment of crisis, with the American invaders at the gates of the city of Quebec, Captain Colin Campbell of the volunteer force known as the royal highland emigrants sailed to St. John's. There, in spite of other demands on the island's manpower for the defence of the port, he succeeded in rallying 180 men to his cause. Quebec was then only a town of 1,000 people and was defended by 100 volunteers. They faced much superior forces from the United States led by Benedict Arnold and Richard Montgomery. Talk of surrender filled the town; in fact all seemed lost until 130 of the Newfoundlanders arrived on the day before Arnold's men appeared at Levis across the river from Quebec. History records Lanctot as saying:
Without the added strength of these 130 fighters -the recruits were all such to a man-the town might have capitulated for an active movement was on foot advocating friendship with the Americans.
The Newfoundlanders made all the difference and Lanctot ended his paper by saying:
Now that Newfoundland has joined the Canadian confederation, it is doubly worthy to recall that the two oldest British colonies have in common the pride of having joined and fought to save Canada from foreign domination.

No one would deny that we have a tradition and a responsibility to the past. But we have also a greater responsibility to the present and to the future. I suggest that responsibility to the past would be best fulfilled by our being true to its real substance and its meaning. Like many others I am concerned about this whole question of national symbols, national anthems, a national flag and all they mean to our country. Yet I am far more concerned with making Canada the kind of country where injustice, grinding poverty, and so on to the best of our ability have been vanquished and where freedom, social justice and equal opportunity for every Canadian can be found, the kind of country which may be proud to have a flag fly.
The union jack will not be abolished, any more than the union jack was abolished when the red ensign was adopted. Canadians, Newfoundlanders or anyone else, cannot be forced to fly any flag. I expect to see the union jack flown now more than at any other time in our history. I can understand the British feelings of the wonderful ladies of the I.O.D.E. I can understand the intensity of the emotion of our gallant war veterans, so honoured in war and so often forgotten in peace. I am not a war veteran. I did enlist, but I was rejected.
I might point out, too, the experience of one of the newest states of the United States, Hawaii. This state, as you know, was at one time British. It is now part of the United States, yet the union jack still proudly flies over all the public buildings in this state.
In my opinion the flag issue will move along these lines. Our new flag will be adopted. This resolution will be passed. Within 50 years, or perhaps much sooner, it will be considered rather odd, rather quaint that Canadians ever lived under a flag that could be confused with that of another country. What will be remembered is that this Prime Minister, Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, of whom so many of us are so very proud, did the job when Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John J. Abbott, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Arthur Meighen, Mackenzie King, Alexander Mackenzie, Sir John Thompson, Sir Charles Tup-per, Sir Robert Borden, R. B. Bennett, Louis St. Laurent and John Diefenbaker did not. It is no easier for him now than it would have been for them. It is my earnest hope, indeed my sincere conviction, that under this distinctive and truly Canadian flag, in which is contained little new and only the best of the very old, Canadians will eventually, at long last, unite.

Canadian Flag

Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty as a member of this house and as the elected representative of the constituency of Wellington-Huron to speak against this resolution and in favour of the amendment calling for a plebiscite.
First, however, I should like to take this opportunity to join other members in the house who congratulated the Minister of Public Works and his department on the beautiful arrangement and display of flags we saw about the lawns of parliament hill for our Dominion day celebration. I cannot but feel that any Canadian who saw that display was proud of that beautiful flag flying as it was yesterday and the day before. I cannot really believe there are many Canadians who would not like to see that display left for the summer period during which the guard is changed in that fine ceremony every morning of the week. Those flags make a beautiful background to the ceremony. The red ensigns, the red coats of the guards and the green grass make a combination of which we can be very proud. I cannot but think that a great many of the people who saw that flag flying did not have in their hearts the hope that it would fly permanently as Canada's distinctive national flag.
Therefore I should like to add my views to those of all hon. members who have spoken before me to plead with the Prime Minister and the government to reconsider the course of action which has been advanced. That course was outlined in the words of the right hon. gentleman when he said "In any event, when the matters I have mentioned are dealt with we shall return to the flag resolutions, and the debate on those resolutions will be continued until a decision is reached".
This reminds me very much of another parliament and another extended debate. I refer to the defence production debate of 1955. Those of us who were here at that time will have vivid recollections of that particular debate in which one of the very distinguished cabinet ministers in this house, a man who had proven himself as a wartime administrator and as one of the greatest organizers of wartime production this country has ever seen, showed that he was not able to change from wartime to peacetime ideals. During the war he had been given extraordinary powers so that he might harness the facilities and production machinery of this nation for military purposes, and his political downfall was due to his failure to adapt to

peacetime circumstances. I refer to the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe who, I repeat, was a distinguished member of this house. The attitude of the Prime Minister, as exemplified in the words I have just quoted, is the attitude which helped bring about the political downfall not only of that fine gentleman but also of the Liberal party in 1957 and 1958.
We all remember some of the phrases coined at that time, and one of the outstanding ones was "If we want to do it, who is going to stop us?" Does this not smack of the words used by the the Prime Minister just the other day? Another well known phrase I can remember the Liberal benches repeating in those days was "We shall let the people decide". This is what is involved in the amendment now before us, that in this great debate we should let the people of Canada decide.
I am reminded of a story I used at that time. It is the story of a traveller who was lost on a back concession of one of our townships one wet, rainy night. He saw a light in the distance, headed for the light, and found refuge in a farmhouse for the night. In the morning he woke up, looked out of the bedroom window and was amazed to see the whole countryside covered with water. He was also amazed at an occurrence which he could not understand; when he looked out the bedroom window he saw a straw hat going up and down, back and forth, in front of the house. When he went downstairs he asked his host for an explanation. The reply was "Oh, that is just grandpappy. Last night before he went to bed he said 'Come hell or high water I am going to cut the grass tomorrow.' " That is the attitude this government is displaying in relation to this flag debate; come hell or high water we are to stay here, whether there is a summer recess or not, until such time as this flag debate is completed.
We also remember how that debate was finally brought to a conclusion. The minister of trade and commerce-the minister of defence production-was conveniently away on government business for two or three days, and during that time the prime minister brought in an amendment limiting the duration of the emergency powers contained in the bill to three years. I am happy to say that when this period expired our party was in power, and nothing more was heard about emergency powers after that.
Mr. Speaker, this is an important debate. It is a debate in which I feel every member

of the house should participate. It is a debate in which all the people of Canada are interested. It would appear that despite all appeals to his better judgment by Canadians of integrity, as well as by many organizations, the Prime Minister intends to proceed to a conclusion with the threat of "no summer recess" hanging over the heads of all members.
My feelings in connection with this issue are well known both in this house and in my constituency. My feelings in favour of the red ensign are well known, because I had a resolution on the order paper last year indicating that I was in favour of the red ensign as Canada's distinctive national flag. I have had tremendous support from my own area in favour of this stand, as is indicated by the many letters I have received from Legion branches, I.O.D.E. groups and other organizations, editorials in weekly newspapers and a resolution from my own county council in the county of Wellington. I may say the council passed the following resolution. I will not quote the entire document; the important part is:
Be it therefore resolved that the council of the corporation of the county of Wellington hereby recommend that the "Canadian red ensign" with the shield of the Canadian coat of arms in the fly be adopted as the national flag of the dominion of Canada and that copies of this resolution be forwarded to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada, the Right Honourable Lester B. Pearson, Prime Minister of Canada, Mr. Maurice Lamon-tagne, Secretary of State, and that further copies be forwarded to the lieutenant governors of all the provinces in the dominion, to Mr. Alfred Hales, M.P. and Mr. Marvin Howe, M.P., to Mr. C. c! Sparline, dominion president of the Royal Canadian Legion and to all county councils in the province of Ontario.
I am happy to say this resolution was endorsed by the other county I represent, the county of Huron. That is an indication that I have the backing of my own people in connection with my stand. However, after talking to many of these people at home I have come to the conclusion that had the Prime Minister carried out the decision he made on May 12, 1964, members of the Legion, members of the I.O.D.E. branches and even my county council would not take precisely the position they do today. I will quote the right hon. gentleman's words. He said:
When the time comes to submit the decision of the government in this matter to the House of Commons I would hope every member of the house would vote as his conscience dictates and that there would be no question of confidence or of non-confidence in a party sense.
As I say, after talking to people in my area I believe that had the Prime Minister agreed
Canadian Flag
to a free vote on this question in the house, and had the new flag which he endorses been approved by the house on that basis, then all the people I have mentioned would have accepted the decision because they believe in the traditions which are associated with those grand old flags, the union jack and the red ensign and, for this reason, they would have accepted a flag which had been approved after a free vote.
However, that is not to be. As has happened so many times, the vacillations, the changing attitudes of this government have been of such a degree that we never know what is coming the next day. Those who talk about the new flag and are in favour of it indicate that there is something in particular ir. the design for new Canadians. They say that the new Canadians who have come to Canada within the last number of years are not in favour of the flag we have at the present time. Once again I can refute that statement with evidence I have from my own riding. I am very happy to say I have received a letter from a lady in one of the communities of my riding. This letter is from Harriston and is dated May 22,	1964,
addressed to me:
I am not in the habit of writing to my member of parliament unless the issue is important. This one is.
It is the issue of a new flag versus the red ensign. It looks like we shall not be given a chance to express our opinion on the flag, because Mr. Pearson intends to keep that one of his election promises.
I am therefore writing to you as the only chance to vote on this issue. I am very much against any new flag and sincerely hope that we will retain the red ensign as our national flag.
As a former German citizen I have not found it difficult, upon becoming a Canadian, to swear my allegiance to this flag and can see no reason for desiring a new one.
My husband also thinks this way. We have no intention of ever flying anything but the red ensign.
Yours very sincerely,
Rita Bedell.
That is a letter from a former German citizen who came to this country in the last few years. I also have before me a petition that was circulated in the village of Drayton. In that village there are a great many people from the Netherlands who have settled there. A great many of the names here endorsing the red ensign are of people who came to this country realizing that this is our national flag. The petition reads as follows:
To: The honourable the House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled
The petition of the undersigned humbly sheweth:

Canadian Flag
That because a meaningful national flag demands the broadest possible acceptance, recognition, and respect
That in the interests of the greatest possible measure of national unity.
They do most earnestly and urgently beseech that the question of a national flag be democratically resolved by granting every Canadian the right to vote on this vital matter by means of a national plebiscite.
And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray.
This is a petition signed by a great many people, as I said, in one of the communities of my riding, and a great many of the names appearing in the petition are of Dutch immigrants.
In connection with this immigration problem and the fact that it has been suggested that these people might be in favour of a new flag, it is interesting to note that all prospective immigrants to Canada have been informed by the department of immigration as follows:
The flag used as distinctive of Canada is properly described as the red ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly. The flag consists of a red field, with the union jack in the first quarter next to the staff. The inclusion of the union jack signifies Canada's association with the other members of the British commonwealth of nations. The coat of arms bears the emblems of the four countries from which the original settlers of Canada were chiefly drawn-the three lions of England, the lilies of France, the lion rampant of Scotland, and the harp of Ireland, together with a branch carrying three maple leaves, the special emblem of Canada.
As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, that is the information given to all prospective immigrants to this country. The Prime Minister has put forth many arguments to condone his actions, one of which is the idea of keeping an election commitment. There were many commitments made, and I am just wondering whether the commitment made by the Minister of Agriculture is going to be kept one of these days. I refer to the commitment to bring in quarterly deficiency payments for agricultural products, which is something that would be of great assistance to the egg producers of Canada at the present time. I well remember how during the election campaign candidates ran up and down the side roads and into the small communities of my area talking about another commitment made on behalf of the Minister of Industry. This was that the Department of Industry was going to bring industry into all the little towns that had been crying for it for years. That was a commitment made by this government, and I wonder when it is going to be kept.
As the hon. member for Marquette said the other day, the highways leading to Ottawa are
[Mr. Howe (Wellington-Huron) .1
paved with election commitments which have never been kept. So the argument that this is an election commitment does not hold any more water than do a great many of the arguments which are being put forward in connection with this flag. This is the reason the Canadian people all across this country are wondering why this legislation is being given such importance at a time when more important matters should be considered. This was pointed out over a year ago in an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of May 22, 1963, headed "A silly issue":
Prime Minister Lester Pearson promised the House of Commons last week that his government will propose the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag within two years. And so, once again, the issue of a national flag has been grasped and promises made-to what end?
Surely we are not so politically immature as to think that keeping or discarding the red ensign or creating an entirely new design is in any way related to the practical degree of our independence. It would be dispiriting to think that people still believe that the loyalty of Canadians would in any way be affected by the colour arrangement on the flag flying on parliament hill.
There are muted suggestions that the separatist tendencies in Quebec might be curbed if the red ensign were replaced by another flag, perhaps with a fleur-de-lis on it. Mr. Pearson should know by now that Quebec cannot be bought, and certainly not with a new flag.
In this age of internationalism the question of a national flag is irrelevant, time-wasting and more than somewhat silly. Mr. Pearson has more important things to deal with than the various ways in which crosses, stripes, and assorted animals and other symbols can be arranged on a piece of cloth.
That article was written over a year ago, and the same thing holds true today. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there is a time for doing things and a time for leaving them alone. The autocratic manner in which this resolution was introduced has definitely created a feeling of animosity throughout the whole country. I was reminded of the debates in 1955 and 1956 when the Prime Minister spoke the other day at the beginning of this debate. I could not help but remember what had been said about trained seals when I heard the regulated applause on that side of the chamber every time the Prime Minister made some announcement in connection with this flag. It reminded me, as I say, of the autocratic, overbearing attitude of that former government, which led to its downfall.
Then there is the question of unity. How much will this new flag add to the unity of Canada? I feel that the actions of this government have not in any way improved the conditions of disunity which seem to have become more grievous since this government

came into power. The royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism, by the very nature of its proceedings and meetings, has done nothing to bring about unity in Canada. This flag debate has aroused feelings of animosity throughout this land which will take generations to heal. I would like to quote from an editorial which appeared in one of the newspapers of my riding. In the issue of the Drayton Advocate for Thursday, May 28 there is an article entitled "The great-grandsons of confederation". This article reads as follows:
Unity should be the ideal of every nation. A disunited nation is an impotent one. Here in Canada the Prime Minister has given as his reason for repudiating the Canadian red ensign that by so doing we will be a more united nation. As his choice of a national flag he tells us it should contain no reference to the British and French founders of this nation. When he talks on the flag issue, Mr. Pearson is emphatic that unity demands a national symbol that makes a clean break with our past.
At other times, and especially in the appointment of the royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism, he tells us we must recognize our great British and French traditions. It is little wonder that the Canadian people find the Prime Minister's assertions confusing. Almost in the same breath he is telling us to recognize our past and at the same time to dismiss it.
The strongest possible reason for retention of the Canadian red ensign is that it recognizes our national roots as an inspiration for the future. Canada has been too unaware of its history A visitor to our newspaper office the other day looked up at the picture of the fathers of confederation that has long hung there and said, it isn t even in our school books now". However, if everything goes amiss at Ottawa, this is Printed the Canadian red +?S!g" "fill be headed for oblivion in the belief that unity will come from a switch in heraldry.
This editorial speaks for itself, Mr. Speaker, and substantiates my argument that this new flag will in no way bring about greater unity in this land of ours.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, 1 appeal once again to the Prime Minister to alter his course of action and allow a free vote to the representatives of the people of Canada, rather than to pursue an overbearing and autocratic course of action which, by promoting symbols which deny our historical, spiritual and national traditions, will not improve the unity of our nation.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I have to speak on this resolution concerning the flag, because I have received more than 5,000 letters from my voters on this matter, asking me to stand up for an exclusively Canadian flag.
Canadian Flag
As an hon. member said here, at the start of this discussion, we are now living historical moments, which will be written in the great book of this country's history as the crucial minutes in which the survival or the agony of Canadian confederation was decided.
In order to place this discussion in its historic context-which, for some, may be somewhat sentimental, but which we all recall with a certain nostalgic feeling-this country was without a flag for many long years and, during the last conflicts, 28 nations pooled their arms, their resources and their human potential for what was called the fight for civilization and freedom.
Each of those countries had its own identity, each was proud of its regiments, its personality and the symbols by which it was represented.
Alas. Canada, a political embryo, England's ill-nurtured offspring, had no distinctive flag. Yet, Canadians were as proud and brave as the other soldiers of other nations. Our feats in battle prove that we were right there in the fray so that other countries might preserve their freedom and their flag, and not be overpowered by the enemy.
When victory came, every country hailed by the crowds carried its own flag, muddy and torn, but the more cherished by the people. Glory and valour took shelter underneath that standard which remained to bear witness.
Canadians, where were we? Did we have the right to remain incognito, when so many sacrifices had been made by the nation as a whole? Should not our politicians have been conscience-stricken when, on parliament hill, among all the flags of the United Nations, the Canadian flag was conspicuous by its absence?
The union jack led Canadians into battle. But the union jack is Great Britain's flag. Salute it proudly, if you wish, but Canada is not England. The union jack cannot be Canada's flag.
As Canadians, we have all paid our debt to our mother countries, and it shows no lack of respect toward the institutions that have guided us to give evidence of maturity today, to show that we have learned our lesson and that, on our own, we are able to organize our structures and our national life at all levels. If we recognize "God Save the Queen" as the royal anthem in Canada, why not recognize "La Marseillaise" or the national anthem of the U.S.A.? If we recognize the union jack, why not recognize the

Canadian Flag
American star spangled banner as a friendly-flag and a tangible evidence of the American economic presence in our country? It is enough for the American people to know that we respect their symbols; it is not necessary to impose them on us to satisfy the fanaticism of some, the ancestral nostalgia of some others and the immaturity of all of them.
But we know that the flag will not be the wealth of the country.
We also know that it will not help Canadians who have run into debt, that it will not give bread to anyone, that it will not protect Canadian families from cold or want, that it will not raise family allowances, and that it will not have any bounteous effect on the country.
The flag will not settle the problem of our farms which are mortgaged up to the hilt, so much so that farmers have to find other employment besides farming. Big landowners will still exploit the people and small landowners will still be money collectors for the exploiters.
We will have, once again, with more determination than ever, under the shade of the flag, to undertake the economic reconquest of Canada; otherwise political reconquest, symbolized by the proposed flag, will only be a faked Canadian emancipation.
We, Canadians, hope that this flag will offend the oppressors, the mealy-mouthed and sanctimonious governments and politicians, the unscrupulous zealous and make them more respectful of justice, so as to restore their rights to the people and their cultural and ancestral heritage to individuals.
We are proud to endorse the resolution concerning a distinctive flag, but we are determined to discard the union jack.
We want "O Canada" as an anthem, but we are unwilling to recognize "God Save the Queen" as Canada's anthem on any score. We shall always honour this flag and this anthem only as those of England.
For us, this new flag is a symbol of hope in the triumph of freedom, and we reject any attempt to hold us back and to compel us to take one step forward while looking back.
In a country where people understand democracy, the problems of the multitude are tackled before the individual interests. We hope that this flag will be a symbol of freedom, security and a vital minimum for all.
[Mr. Latulippe.l
Many Canadians who are living here remain fond of other countries. To accept two flags and two national anthems in Canada would justify the stand of separatists and many Canadians who cannot bear a compromise not to say degradation.
For a thing to be distinctive it must be without any connection, independent, free and a complete whole in itself. Such is not the case of the proposed flag, since the acceptance of two flags suggests the idea of dependence.
It is useless to try to deceive the people. With that second flag, we dress up the Canadian political skeleton which remains without substance. Until we repatriate the constitution to break any direct link with England, our symbols of an adult Canadian life will remain only smokescreens in front of a half dead colonial reality which still has some trembling movements.
We have proven today to the other countries of the world that we lack political maturity, that our initiative is limited to motherly instructions, that we are still only colonials dreaming of national unity but who, caught at their own game, do not have the necessary maturity to get for themselves the essential tools to acquire that unity, namely the conscience of a Canadian entity without ties and without compulsion.
Let this flag be the hope that our common efforts to build a united Canadian nation, in line with international and national realities, will be put in concrete form, a symbol that could endear itself to all Canadians regardless of their origin.
Adapting to this debate the words of the late President Kennedy, I say: Let us ask ourselves not what this flag can do for us but what we can all do for the flag, particularly for what it must stand for, a proud and united Canada, a Canada aware of her national life.
For some years now, French Canada has been playing an increasingly greater part among modern nations. New responsibilities must therefore be assumed by our people.
It must cultivate the wisdom to give without vexing others and to receive without giving up any of itself. For a nation which has reached adulthood, it means taking conscience of itself before others. It means going on with the dialogue between equals, starting new exchanges.
Since the French Canadian nation has decided to develop more than ever its numerous resources and to expand as much as

possible, while taking into account its collective responsibility, it must show great respect for the whole of mankind while doing it; to become what we are, we must be attracted by what we are not.
One is different only with regard to others, and to serve them the whole of Canada must develop its own personality so that its human values can express themselves for the greater benefit of all after everyone's contribution has been added to them.
Therefore, the love of the nation for that flag must be actively encouraged. The progress of institutions working for the advancement of other nations must also take place in that concept.
Of course, we must first of all be charitable to our neighbour.
That flag should help us to remember all those underdeveloped nations where man lives under conditions which are indeed a denial of his dignity.
That noble flag should really fulfil the true yearnings of the nation, but justice does not simply mean to refrain from doing wrong to others; it means also to help them to the best of our ability.
If a nation really wants to be strong and respected, it must serve at all times the cause of justice, claiming its rights with energy and respecting with equity the rights of others.
The Canadian nation, because of its particular political situation, cannot turn a deaf ear to the cause of justice.
On that score, an investigation of the exact nature of our cultural and political community is required as a necessary preamble. We must also try to establish and take advantage as clearly as possible of the legitimate aspirations of the nation.
Highly qualified men must try to discover all the implications and possibilities of unalienable rights and strive for recognition of those that have not been asserted, regain those which may have been withdrawn. Everyone must strive always to respect the dignity of others in this fight for one's rights.
A true and authentic patriotism which respects justice requires that each citizen honestly accomplish his daily task.
Any claim respecting rights which ignores the corrective duties may end up in a frightful hoax. It is only when each individual carries out his work with competence, when his intentions are pure and when his work is continuous that a people can claim its rights. Justice cannot be established in passion and confusion.
Canadian Flag
This, hon. members, is of perspective in which we should envisage this matter of establishing a distinctive Canadian flag, as a serious-minded member should do, a member who wants a flag that will represent something true to his people, that will symbolize all the greatness and the nobility of his heart and mind.
We should stop being bellowing politicians, hungering for votes, and we should try to be statesmen, hungering for the welfare of our people and the greatless of our country. Is that not, for each one of us, the mandate entrusted to its representatives by the nation?

Mr. Speaker, my personal feelings about the flag are quite simple. They are summed up in those immortal words we used as school children: "The maple leaf, our emblem dear, the maple leaf forever". I shall not however break forth into song on this occasion.
The old version?

Whether the flag should have one maple leaf, as has been suggested, a cluster of three maple leaves or something that has not yet been widely canvassed, 10 leaves, is of less moment than the basic maple leaf concept itself. Ten leaves actually might be rather good. For one thing, such a flag would enable us to add more leaves should the spirit of manifest destiny seize this nation once again. For another thing, I think, 10 leaves would give greater scope for artistic expression, although I realize that members of parliament should not go too far in the sphere of artistic expression after our world fair symbol experience.
I am quite happy, very happy in fact, with the cluster of three maple leaves. The fact that it has historic and heraldic significance, as has been pointed out many times in the house, the fact also that it has the sanction of nature, seem to me decisive. However, the fact that I personally prefer the maple leaf concept, and in particular a cluster of three maple leaves, is not of course really relevant. Like all of us, I have been getting a great number of letters both pro and con on this subject, and the fact that a great number of my constituents prefer and favour the maple leaf concept is surely not the main point either. As has been stated by speakers on both sides of the house in this debate, the main point is surely that we adopt in this house that flag which will unify and not divide us as a nation. This is the

Canadian Flag
crux of the whole issue it seems to me, and indeed so many speakers have referred to this that my feeling is that the majority of members regard the basic question as what will help most to unify Canada, what will least divide us-
Drop the subject.

-as by far the most important question. We as members of parliament are here to make a decision on this matter, as we try to do on all other matters in the economic, social and other spheres. It is particularly important in a matter like the flag because, as we all know, a flag is and must be a national symbol. It must say something to all parts of the nation. Above all, it must not go totally against the grain of any significant part of the nation.
I submit that the new maple leaf flag does not go totally against the grain of any large part of the nation. I realize that it is not universally loved. Many of my constituents have written to tell me that they would prefer to have the red ensign. My constituency is a largely Anglo-Saxon one. Indeed, my own people on my mother's side settled there in the late 18th century as United Empire Loyalists. But what I have noticed from my correspondence and from my conversations, and they have been many, with the supporters of the red ensign in Northumberland is that, with the exception of a very few, they are prepared to accept the new flag rather than have a flag which is not acceptable to a large, significant and important part of our nation.
I must confess that there are a very few who are rabidly anti-French, almost rabidly raceistic, if there is such a word. As the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock) pointed out the other day, and I entirely agree, the concept of racism can be carried dangerously far. We have people in English speaking and French speaking Canada alike who have this kind of herrenvolk attitude. However, except for a very few in this category the red ensign supporters who have written me about their feelings in regard to the flag have invariably said that it is true they love the red ensign and would not like to have to switch their allegiance, but would rather do so than to have a flag not acceptable to a large and important part of our nation.
Surely it is better to choose the flag that will divide us the least. It seems to me this is the only really important point. I am not suggesting that the only Canadians who favour the new flag are the five and a half

million French speaking Canadians to whom I have referred. Indeed, as we all well know, this is not the case. Judging from my correspondence it is obvious that a large majority of young people prefer the new flag. I have also found that new Canadians, although not universally, generally feel the same way. If we read the ethnic press carefully we can ascertain that they would prefer a new flag. But above all the young people, the people of tomorrow in all parts of Canada, feel strongly about the maple leaf concept, and they are the ones who will be waving the flag when we are all dead and gone from this chamber.
You will be gone before you are dead.

In other words, Mr. Speaker, to adopt the new flag rather than the red ensign would not, it seems to me, deeply alienate any large cultural group in Canada, whereas to adopt the red ensign or some modification of it would. Let us face it. We all know that to do so would alienate deeply and permanently, I fear, a large and important section of this one Canada. We do not need a referendum to tell us that. All a referendum would do would be to exacerbate our cultural diversities.
In the last 97 years Canada in my view has moved a long way toward becoming a strong and united nation. We have become much more an economically integrated nation. We have found increasingly that our social problems are ones that touch us from coast to coast. I am not suggesting that we have become a uniform nation either in the social or economic spheres, but we all know that we have increasingly moved a very long way toward a national unity, toward a unity which does have, as I say, common problems in the economic and social spheres right across this nation.
In one area, however, we have not it seems to me, and I am glad we have not, found ourselves becoming entirely nationally integrated. This is in the area of cultural traditions and outlook. One of our trouble spots, it is true, but surely one of our great strengths, something that enriches us all, has been and is our cultural diversity.
I suggest that we could go on and have an even greater expression of cultural diversity, not only amongst those who came here in the 18th century or earlier but amongst the many who have come to Canada since. We could have a great deal of cultural diversity, and at the same time

move toward trying to achieve those things that all Canadians need and want in the social and economic spheres.
We must, however, take special care when it comes to discussing any matter that is directly within the cultural arena. Such a matter is, of course, a national flag. It is on this ground, and on this ground alone therefore that I think we, as members of parliament, should look at this whole question, regardless of our personal feelings in the matter, regardless even of what we think the majority of our constituents want. In English speaking Canada, most of us find that our constituents are sharply divided on this matter. Regardless of these things, important though they are our personal feelings and the divided views of our constituents the important thing for all of us as members of parliament, it seems to me, is to pursue that policy which, as I have said, will divide us least and will help, I am convinced, to unify us even more in the future.
A referendum, Mr. Speaker, is only really suitable in a culturally and socially homogeneous society. I, personally, do not object to it so much because it is contrary to parliamentary democracy-although in fact it is. As important as this is, I object to a referendum because all it will do will be to reveal more sharply our cultural diversities, our strong feelings on this matter. All it will do will be to alienate still further a very large number of Canadians, French speaking Canadians. Whether we like it or not, French speaking Canadians are people who have lived in this nation a long time; are people with whom we share this nation and who are particularly strongly of the view that a distinctive, new Canadian flag is the right thing for us. They are not the only ones who feel this way, as I have said. I feel this way and many others feel this way too. But the fact that they do, the fact that to go against their feelings would be to split our nation asunder, seems to me to be the only really crucial point.
May I ask the hon. lady a question?

I have just about finished.
Finally, there is the question, why act now? We all know that the problem of a national flag is not a new one. We all know that whenever it has been discussed it was difficult to reach a decision on it. We all know that all parties in this house have spoken about it for some years. It is really not new. We all know, too, that there is going to be a substantial amount of time for discussion in
Canadian Flag
this house, and for all the groups in society that have strong views on this matter to get their views across. One cannot deny that the groups in society that do have strong views on this subject have had enormous opportunities, and are continuing to have those opportunities, to get their views across. This is important. I think it is vital in any democracy. It seems to me that if we make this decision this summer, given the time we have for debate, given the time there is for those outside interests to present their views to us, we ought surely to be able to make our decision here which we feel is in the best interests of this nation. After all, it was this nation for which we fought in the second world war, and the values for which it stands. It was not a particular flag for which we fought; it was for freedom, tolerance and understanding, and a respect for minority rights. These are the things for which we fought. These are the things we maintain, and I hope will continue to maintain.
I wonder if the hon. lady would permit the question I wished to pose earlier?
Yes.
Does the hon. lady feel the same sentiments in regard to the acceptance or non-acceptance of the red ensign should apply to the union jack, as provided for in the second portion of this resolution?

Mr. Speaker, this is not a debate on the second part of the resolution. The second part of the resolution is not to create a national flag for Canada. All I am concerned about is the creation of a national flag for Canada.
May I ask the hon. lady a question? What evidence has the hon. lady that the ethnic press is clamouring for this new maple leaf flag?
I have not got it here, but I will be glad to send it to the hon. gentleman.
Has the hon. member any clippings or quotations?
Yes, and I will be glad to send them to the hon. member later.
I think it would be worth while to put them on the record, as I did.

I shall be glad to do that if I get another opportunity in the course of the debate.

Canadian Flag

I should like to say a few words at this particular time in this debate in support of the amendment and in opposition to the resolution before the house. I think, Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss if I did not, at this time, say a few words on behalf of the constituents of the London riding. It is not the largest in Canada, but it is one of the largest. It is a completely urban riding. I know that the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. Millar) and the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) have made surveys in their respective ridings which adjoin mine. These surveys have not produced results exactly the same as mine, and this is understandable because they are different types of ridings.
However, I did make a survey through the medium of broadcasting. I sent out word to the people of my riding that they should communicate with me by letter, telephone or whatever means suited them best, and let me know what their feelings are with regard to the flag. I received some 842 letters. Of that number, 824 were opposed to the new flag as proposed. The vast majority were in favour of the retention of the red ensign. I know that some of these letters I have received may have reached me as a result of the efforts of an organization, a group of people who got together and decided they would make representations. So I will cut the number I gave in two. Suppose half these letters were inspired. If we do that, then the majority is still 23 to 1 in favour of the retention of the red ensign, and on that basis it does not take much imagination for me to establish exactly which way I should go in the interests of the people who have elected me as their representative here.
Of the remaining 18 letters, 17 were in favour of a new flag. Perhaps I might say that even the 18 were. Nine of these were not in favour of the flag as proposed. The other writer I mentioned told me what he thought would be a good flag; he described it to me, but parliamentary language does not permit me to tell the house exactly what it was.
However, I would say this: Before we have another national flag-and I think I should say "another" because we already have one- it would be a good idea if we approached full nationhood. There are some things which are lacking. I had occasion recently to pick up a passport on the inside of which were words to the effect that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and Queen Elizabeth II grant the passport and offer the

bearer certain privileges. If we look further into this passport-which is not a Canadian passport; it is a British passport-we find the words "A Canadian subject is a British subject". These are some of the details to which we should address attention before we lay claim to complete and full nationhood and go on to change the flag we already have for something new. Then again, on the applications for employment we have in this country, some of them governmental, appears a column asking details of nationality. If you put down "Canadian" in that column, in most instances the application is returned because they want to know the racial origin. This is one of the things which I contend is causing great disunity in this country and it is something we are condoning. As I say, we must first reach the point of complete and legitimate nationhoood.
To think in terms of hyphenated Canadians is I think completely wrong. I do not think we should refer to people as Ukrainian Canadians, Dutch Canadians, German Canadians and so on. I do not think anyone should be considered in that way. Once people have taken out citizenship papers in this country they are Canadians and we should do everything we can within our power to make them proud of this country. I feel I am a Canadian, not a hyphenated Canadian in any sense of the word. After six generations I feel I am almost as Canadian as a full blooded Indian, and I am very proud of the fact. On the other hand, these people who come to us from various countries for the protection-I was about to say of the red ensign, but I will not say that-these people who come to our shores for the protection they receive in Canada so that they may live in peace and harmony, all bring to us a certain amount of their culture. We are pleased to have this so that eventually we may be in possession of aspects of all these cultures, put them together and, as a result, have our own distinctive Canadian culture.
I feel that one of the things which is incensing the people of Canada today is the manner in which this resolution has been presented. I think this is something the people are concerned about. We have a freedom loving people in Canada and they do not like to see this sort of thing shoved down their throats and enforced in a dictatorial manner. One of the other things which I feel is puzzling the people of Canada at this moment is the fact that members on the other side of the house do not have an opportunity of voting freely on this issue. They cannot have the opportunity of a free vote. The Prime

Minister said recently that he hoped everybody would vote as they pleased. On the other hand he said later that the government stands or falls on the fate of this particular resolution. In such a situation how can those on the other side of the house vote against their leader, vote against the government and bring about the dissolution of this parliament? These are things to which the people of Canada take severe exception.
The Prime Minister was once considered to be one of the greatest diplomats in the world. He was a man of whom we were particularly proud in that capacity. Indeed he received a high award for the services he rendered in that field. I know that hon. members on the other side of the house, as well as some who sit elsewhere-and I am going to count myself among them-were proud of him. But, Mr. Speaker, what has happened? There is no diplomacy in the manner in which this resolution has been presented. There is no democracy about the way in which it has been presented. On the other hand, the Prime Minister gave us all an invitation to speak on this subject in the house and I am just wondering whether, after what could run into a great length of time, someone will have the temerity to turn round and say: "This is a filibuster". It cannot be. This was an invitation addressed by the Prime Minister to each and every one of us to get on our feet and express our views on behalf of our constituents.
What was the right hon. gentleman looking for? What was in the back of his mind? Let us think about this for a moment. Was this a way out? Was he looking for some way to back out of this, or was this a smokescreen to cover up the ineptness of the present administration? Was it possibly because of trouble in the commission on biculturalism and bilingualism? Did he want to cover that up in a cloud? Was it put forward as a smokescreen to cover up the increasing economic difficulties of this country? We could cite many possibilities. Was it to force an election before it was too late? Maybe the right hon. gentleman thought the sands of time were running out. Maybe he thought the proverbial chickens were coming home to roost and that he had better have an election now, because in the spring it would be too late. I am wondering about these things and I think we should give them careful thought.
There are three ways in which this flag proposition could have been approached, in
Canadian Flag
my humble view, and I will list them though not necessarily in order of importance. The first is by way of a federal-provincial conference to which the premiers of each of the provinces and select small committees could have been invited, to sit with a full committee representing all five parties in this house around the conference table to produce something which would be acceptable to at least a majority of the people. Then the people, through their representatives, would have the opportunity of exercising a freedom of choice. I submit this freedom of choice is being denied.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, there is an educational approach to this question. In the last general election campaign the Prime Minister mentioned that there would be 1,000, 10,000-it does not matter about the figure, because we have not had them, anyway- awards for students. Why did we not turn this whole problem over to the educational authorities in this country and say to each educational district, "Have the students in your area submit what they think would be the proper design for a distinctive Canadian flag". They could then have selected two or three of these designs, sent them to the central headquarters of the district, and the committee of the house I have mentioned could have picked out the six best designs. We could have awarded $1,000 each to the students who submitted what we thought were the best designs. That would have been a great deal cheaper than spending $100,000 a day for this house to sit in the discussion of this problem and we would have given the students an opportunity to take part in the choice of a flag, to express themselves in this connection, to become more patriotic and better Canadians.
The third manner in which this question could be handled is by a plebiscite or referendum. I would like to suggest a few words that could be put into the questionnaire on this particular subject, although I do not suggest the questions should be asked necessarily in this order. The questionnaire could be worded something like this:
1.	Are you in favour of the design of three maple leaves joined on one stem, on a white background?
2.	Are you in favour of retaining the red ensign as Canada's national flag?
3.	Do you favour a change in the red ensign by removing the coat of arms and substituting therefor a maple leaf and fleur-de-lis?
4.	Do you favour a national flag with neither union jack nor fleur-de-lis thereon?

Canadian Flag
There could be added one or two more questions. But at least, Mr. Speaker, we would get a true expression of the opinions of people on this matter and they would have the opportunity of saying what they wanted by way of a flag. In this way we would be getting back somewhat to democracy. On the other hand, why should we be treated like children? This is a most unreasonable thing. Why should the hammer be placed over our heads in the form of, "You pass this resolution or you get no summer recess". As far as I am concerned, I am prepared to sit here all summer.
Hear, hear.

I do not care whether we have a recess or not. But let us put before this house some legislation which we can handle, and let this issue sit for a while. Then we could come back to it later, when it could be considered a little more dispassionately. The way this issue has been thrown at us is indicative of, "You be good boys and you will have a holiday", and it reminds me of the little boy who had a ball and bat and went up to the playground, gathered all the other boys around him, and wanted to be the pitcher. They did not want him to be the pitcher, and he said, "All right. I will take my ball and bat and go home". I cannot see the wisdom of the manner in which this matter has been handled; it is very difficult to understand.
There is something else we must face, Mr. Speaker. We cannot go around like the proverbial ostrich, with our heads buried in the sand forever. There are some things we have to face. One of the things we have to face, whether we like it or not, is the separatist movement in Quebec. I know this is not indicative of the feeling of the majority of people in Quebec by any means, but still it is there and we have to face it. I think we would find the majority of these people to be in the age bracket 18 to 24. So six years from today, if we are still together then, these people will be in the age bracket 18 to 30, and this represents a great proportion of the population of Canada. This is something that is very serious; it is of major importance- and we cannot afford blindly to look away from it.
I think it is time our Prime Minister-who is known for his diplomatic prowess; who is known to be a great statesman: we will not say anything about his ability as an administrator-approached the premier of Quebec and obtained a commitment from him that they are going to be with us in 1967 when we have

our centennial celebrations. If we do not obtain that commitment, I say let us get a new site, and get it now, before we start pouring millions and millions more dollars into this particular site.
Get back on the flag.

What is the result? Confusion; complete and utter confusion. Two new flags have been suggested to the house. We have one old flag which we have been using for some time and which was officially endorsed. There is a move afoot whereby the province of Ontario may opt out of this flag, just the same as Quebec opted out of the pension plan in its original form. If they opt out, we will get four flags. And there could be other provinces that will decide they want their own flag. Perhaps the province of Quebec will decide to fly their provincial flag. We could end up with 12 flags. What confusion and what disunity.
This is a real problem, one that cannot be handled on the spur of the moment. This is a problem on which we will have to take a little time and perhaps do a little compromising. What we are doing now is continually driving wedges between groups of people, driving them further and further apart. This is nothing new, and I would like to refer hon. members to the House of Commons Debates of 1900, 64 years ago. I shall read from from volume 1 of the debates of that year, page 1842, half way down the right-hand column. These are the words of a very outstanding man of this house at that time, the first officer of this house, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I might preface this by saying that these words were spoken in reply to a statement made by, I believe, the attorney general of that time. This was in the debate on supply with regard to sending troops to South Africa. The prime minister said this:
It is only too true, sir, that if we had refused at that time to do what was in my judgment our imperative duty, a most dangerous agitation would have arisen-an agitation which according to all human probability would have ended in a cleavage in the population of this country upon racial lines. A greater calamity could never take place in Canada. My hon. friend and I have long been on terms of intimacy. He has long been a political friend and supporter of mine. He knows as well as any man in this house knows that if there is anything to which I have given my political life, it is to try to promote unity, harmony and amity between the diverse elements of this country.
My friends can desert me, they can remove their confidence from me, they can withdraw the trust which they have placed in my hands; but never shall I deviate from that line of policy. Whatever may be the consequences, whether loss of prestige, loss of popularity, or loss of power, I feel that I am in the right, and I know that a time will

come when every man, my hon. friend himself included, will render me full justice on that score... We are a British country and a free country, and every man in it has the right to express his opinion.
Those were the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1900.
In the Montreal Gazette for October 22, 1963 there is a letter which contains a quotation from Sir Wilfrid Laurier which is as follows:
I am proud of the country that gave me birth-
-and the letter indicates he was referring to Canada-
-and I am proud of the country that gave me liberty-
-referring to Britain. Mr. Speaker, this is the kind of Canadian, one of the greatest of all times, that the Liberal party presented to the house in 1900, or a little before then. What a change we have today; times have changed. We have a flag now which I am sure is acceptable to the vast majority of the people of Canada, so why change it? After the next election when we have a new government another flag resolution may be brought in, and then we will have more confusion and the same trouble all over again. I do not think a new government would do that but it could happen. We should remember that we are all Canadians and that we should get together in a spirit of unity, and in a spirit of compromise work something out which would be satisfactory to the vast majority of our people.
I should like to quote another item which I think is very interesting. It originates from "Viewpoint", a show with which I am sure all are familiar. On June 16, 1964 this statement was made by Mr. Robert Needham of the press gallery:
But, whatever the merits of the tri-leaf, the red ensign or any other flag, I cannot conceive of poorer circumstances under which a supposed emblem of unity is being presented to the nation.
What other conclusion is possible, when a splintered house is held hostage by a minority government. A distinctive flag now-or a general election. That's the choice. That's the ransom demanded of a captive commons.
Such is the birth and baptism in bondage decreed for a flag of freedom.
Now let me go to another man whom I presume some people have heard about. His name is Newman; I think his first name is Peter. He has written other articles, but the one to which I wish to refer is in the July 4 issue of Maclean's magazine. He starts off: Just after Lester Pearson became the fourteenth prime minister of Canada, he described his stewardship, in a television address, as "a time to
Canadian Flag
excite the daring, test the strong and give new promise to the timid"...
Now. 14 months later, it is evident even to the Liberals that their administration has yet to earn the title to these brave words. What may be less evident, althought here in Ottawa it seems clear enough to me, is that in the day-to-day business of governing the country the Liberals are falling short of even the most basic demand made on any government: that the administration control events and shape the course of national affairs ... But it seems to me that on almost any afternoon of this session there has been some evidence to be seen in the house of vacillation and retreat... in my opinion the domestic policies of the Liberals have been a grey, quiet failure.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is this. Why should we be wasting so much time when there is so much legislation we should be getting on with? Why do we not set this measure back for a while, give it a chance to simmer and let the people look at it from a sensible sort of viewpoint rather than push it through now? Let us debate this question of the flag later. Our present flag or any new flag which might possibly be, I will not say forced upon us, but any new flag we might acquire through a pressure medium, should stand for justice, for freedom and for liberty. But most of all it should stand for unity, and I do not see where this proposed measure will inspire any unity in any part of the country. It should represent further the sacrifices which were made by our forefathers when they forged for us from a vast continent a new country where we might live together as individuals in freedom; where we might enjoy freedom of choice, freedom of worship and freedom of speech regardless of race, colour or creed. I say long may this freedom live, Mr. Speaker. Let us proceed slowly. What we do today we have to live with for a long time. Let us go back to the days of trade and barter and perhaps we can compromise a little and get together on this matter. But whatever we do, let us not break faith with the people of Canada. Let us give them an opportunity to express themselves individually, in line with the amendment to the resolution before us today.
