Let us shelve this question temporarily and look at it from a dispassionate point of view. Meantime, let us get on with the business of Canada. Our constituents sent us here to legislate, so let us go to work on legislation, and let the flag sit so that we may get together on the matter a little later on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business

Motions for Papers
as listed on today's order paper, namely private bills, notices of motions (papers), public bills.

That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all government statements and directives to government departments during the past year regarding security procedures and investigations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am not only surprised but I admit I am bitterly disappointed that I have to move this motion. On a number of occasions since I came to this house some two years ago the house has discussed the whole policy of security matters, the rights of people who work for the government to know what they are accused of-if they are accused-and their right to an opportunity to give their side of the story, in other words an opportunity to defend themselves.
This matter has been raised not only by members of parliament but by organizations such as the Canadian association of university teachers and the Canadian union of students representing all the students in Canadian universities. Last session we thought we had finally got a policy from the government, a policy which was fair, which would protect the rights of government employees and which would ensure that justice would be theirs.
I wish to quote a couple of paragraphs from what I thought was a very important statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in this house on October 25, 1963. Members will find this on pages 4043 to 4046 of Hansard for that date. In it he said:
If our security policies ignored, or did not take sufficiently into account, the basic rights of the individual, they could operate not to defend but to destroy the liberties which are our first concern.
Later he said:
The first of the new requirements is to inform the person involved when his security or reliability is in doubt and may have to involve his dismissal. Employing departments and agencies will in future be required to tell an employee everything that is possible of the reasons for the doubt, if there is a doubt, and to give him an opportunity to resolve that doubt...
The second new requirement is to ensure that a second look is always taken by a separate body before dismissal is finally decided upon. Once the individual is told of security doubts he will have the opportunity to give his side of the case.

Finally he said:
1	feel confident that the procedure which we are now adopting will assist us in making judgments concerning loyalty and reliability in a manner which will protect individual rights as well as national interests.
That was an excellent statement. The Prime Minister always makes excellent statements when he talks in broad generalities, but when you try to pin him down to anything you find there is not much in it. He made this statement and he met with representatives of the Canadian association of university teachers. I see the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) here. She was at that meeting. The Prime Minister gave that organization assurances that the government would work out satisfactory policies, that it would keep in touch with the organization, and hold discussions with it in future. I am told that as of today the members of that organization have not heard a further word from the Prime Minister.
On May 7 of this year I asked the following question:
1.	Has the new policy regarding security investigations promised by the Prime Minister last session been established and, if not, how long will it be before it is ready?
2.	If it has been completed and approved, have its terms been made known to the employees of the government and their associations?
3.	Will a copy of the policy and its regulations be tabled in the house?
The answer to that question came down on May 25 last and was as follows:
1. Yes.
2	and 3. The terms have been formally communicated to all government departments and organizations. It is not customary to send directives such as this to employees or associations, nor are administrative directives normally tabled in. the House of Commons.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, this is precisely the reason we have had this kind of difficulty, because security is not just the business of the government ministers and their departments. Security is the business of the people involved. It is the business of all members in this house, and if the members of this house and the people in the Canadian association of university teachers and the Canadian union of students had been satisfied with the former ring-around-a-rosy which we had between the government, the R.C.M.P. and other people, we would never have had these discussions; but the fact is that the policies have not worked out, and many mistakes were made.
I refer hon. members to the Knott case, raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Co-wichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) in which the government, because of the evidence

presented to it, was forced to admit that a mistake had been made. It admitted Knott had been dismissed from the navy because his uncle was a member of the communist party, and then it admitted a mistake had been made because in fact the person in the communist party was not his uncle.
I want to ask the Minister of Justice this question. Supposing his uncle had been a member of the communist party, what had that to do with the man in the navy? Have we reached the situation in this country when a person is judged guilty not because of what he does himself but because of what his relatives may have done or may be arguing?
If that is the kind of procedures we have, then we have taken a leaf out of the book of nazi Germany, because it had this kind of law. Nazi Germany enacted a law which, in rough translation, was entitled a law dealing with the clan responsibility. Under that law when a person committed a crime against the security of the state every person in his family, his father, his mother, his sister, his brother, his uncle, his aunt and his cousins to the 'nth degree were adjudged to be equally responsible. I am not saying we have that kind of law here. If we had, then we could fight it, but what we have had are administrative procedures exactly like those which were followed in nazi Germany.
I have talked about the Knott case which was settled satisfactorily, and following that we had the Petersen case. Eric Petersen of Esquimalt, B.C., had been a member of the navy for ten years and, according to himself and his counsel, he was dismissed from the navy. The reason given was that his father-in-law was a communist, but the fact is that his father-in-law was a communist when Petersen was one year old.
I asked questions about this in the house and got the usual run-around which always takes place when one gets into security matters because, after all, an ordinary backbencher cannot be expected to understand the fine points of security. This is for that select group, the Minister of Justice, his assistant, other people around him and the R.C.M.P. When I did not make any progress I went to see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) who told me very plainly that this was not the reason Petersen had been dismissed from the navy. He said they had other reasons, good reasons; but I can tell the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) that the Minister of National Defence did not tell them to me, and I am satisfied that until today Petersen has not been told why he was dis-
Motions for Papers
missed from the navy, so that he could really defend himself. He has to take the word of some faceless accuser that they have information which makes it necessary for him to be dismissed from the navy.
Last session I had a letter from a young man in my constituency, who told me he belonged to the naval reserve for three years and when he and his friends, with whom he had served in the naval reserve for three years, went to reinlist, his friends were taken back in but he was turned down. I asked him to call on me and I spent an hour with him in Winnipeg going over the possible reasons. I got the assurance from him that he had never belonged to any organization which could possibly be classed as subversive. He told me all the organizations to which he belonged. However, having had some experiences in these cases, which I would be very happy not to have had, I asked him about the members of his family, and it came out that his father worked for an organization which I am sure the government would consider to be communist dominated.
Let us assume for the moment that his father was a communist 20 years ago or even that his father is communist today. Is there anybody here who is going to suggest that because a person's father is or was a communist that person therefore ought not to be able to be a member of the naval reserve? We are not talking about atomic research or nuclear bombs. We are talking about an ordinary seaman.
I am not going to mention this person's name because he did not authorize me to discuss the matter publicly, but what about the person who wanted to work for the C.B.C. and who was turned down because his father allegedly is a comunist? This is precisely the kind of thing that has gone on and I am satisfied it is still going on. I will believe it is going on until the government realizes that if they really have a new policy there is nothing wrong with telling the house about it, and also telling the organizations representing employees and the people of Canada what that policy is.
I never wanted and I do not want today to know the details. I do not want to see the actual questions which are asked. I am not really concerned about the answers. I am not concerned about every position in the government which requires security clearance. But surely to goodness there can be nothing wrong with the government making a clear policy statement in a broad way of what the requirements are, what departments

Motions for Papers
require security clearance, what the reasons are and what kind ol matters are involved in security. Until we have this type of procedure there are going to be complaints and members of the house and people outside the house are going to continue to ask questions and to be critical.
We have heard all the arguments why there cannot be an independent group to look into these matters. We have suggested such a body. We have suggested that if the government is going to lift the security clearance of any person employed by it that person should be told first of all that he is losing his security clearance. Second, he should be given some indication of what the general reasons for such action are. Third, he should have an opportunity to explain, to make a defence.
If such a practice should be adopted I will not be satisfied and the members of this group will never be satisfied if the only people to whom the employee can make his explanation are people in his own department. These is no reason at all why there cannot be an independent semi-judicial review committee. I point out to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) that during world war II when the defence of Canada regulations were in effect, not in a time of peace but during a war when thousands of people were interned-I am not questioning the necessity of that for a moment-provision was made for a review committee to which people who had been interned and thought they had been unfairly treated could make representations. I understand that committee had on it a representative of the judiciary and it was empowered to hear not only the government's side of the story but to hear the defence, the explanations of the people involved. It also had power to recommend that people who had been interned should be allowed to go free. If we could do that in wartime surely we can do it in peacetime.
I want to say that the kind of answer the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) gave to my question was most unsatisfactory. I had been assured before by the Prime Minister's office that he was sympathetic to my motion to produce this material but that the security people were unhappy about it. It is obvious that the security people persuaded the Prime Minister that he could not do this. That is precisely the sort of thing to which I object.
The Prime Minister and the government indulge in fine talk, though in generalities, when they want the support of organizations like the Canadian association of university

teachers. The question of security procedures at universities is a separate one which we will also be pressing. But we got this very nice answer from the Prime Minister who likes to think of himself as a liberal with a small "1". When the chips are down, however, when it comes time for action, when it comes time to tell the security people and the R.C.M.P. that maybe they are going to have to explain to somebody besides themselves, the Prime Minister loses his courage and we get the kind of nonsense we had in the refusal of the government to table these directives. If the Prime Minister could not table the directives he could have made a statement explaining to members of the house and the public what the situation is with regard to security.
I said in opening my remarks that I was sorry I had to raise this matter. I assure the Minister of Justice that unless we receive a good deal more information that we have got up to now this matter will be another one on which we will have to spend a lot more time at this session than it should take simply because the government has not got the guts to take the people into its confidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that during the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Justice on October 25, 1963, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said, as reported on page 4043 of Hansard for that day:
The security measures which have been developed here in Canada, through sometimes bitter experience, are intended to be preventive and not punitive. Their purpose is to protect the safety, interests and indeed the freedoms of all Canadians. They are under constant and continuous review, with the purpose of striking the balance I have referred to between the protection of the state and the protection of the individuals who, in a free society, alone give the state its direction, its purpose and indeed its meaning.
He said further, as reported on page 4044:
The granting or the denial of a security clearance is an administrative matter, one of managerial responsibility. In making a decision that an applicant or employee may not safely be given access to secret and confidential information, the head of a department or of an agency is not denying an individual a right. No person, of course, has a right to see official secrets. The department head is merely exercising the judgment he is expected to apply on the basis of all the information available to him in the way that any sensible person would exercise such judgment in hiring a secretary, a cashier, a lawyer or a doctor, ensuring that such person could be trusted with his property, his private business or his physical health. The government also has an obligation to provide itself with every reasonable assurance that those of its employees who require access to the government's, the nation's secrets are loyal and trustworthy and not vulnerable to persuasion, coercion or blackmail.

I feel confident that the procedures which we are now adopting will assist us in making judgments concerning loyalty and reliability in a manner which will protect individual rights as well as national interests.
Following the statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made at that time the then minister of justice went on to outline in some detail the security screening arrangements which had been devised. At that time he said, as reported on page 4046 of Hansard:
I do so with some reluctance because the effectiveness of even these measures is usually reduced in providing information about them. At the same time, I fully appreciate how frustrating it is to members of this house as well as to the public generally, who are rightly concerned that individuals be treated fairly, to be faced with official silence on this vital subject. There will always be matters in this area which cannot be discussed fully in public if our defensive arrangements are to have any effect at all. I am sure all members of the house will agree with the principle of that statement. On the other hand, the effectiveness of these arrangements does not depend solely upon the measures or the individuals involved with them. They depend too upon the understanding and cooperation of all Canadians on whose behalf, in the last analysis, these measures have been instituted.
It was the purpose of this statement, Mr. Speaker, to explain to the house, and to all Canadians, in as much detail as was consistent with national security and the general interest, the means by which the government intends to safeguard these vital secrets as well as the rights and interests of its employees in this regard. These statements were, I believe, the fullest which any government of Canada has ever made on this difficult subject. They were made in the knowledge that they would probably lead to demands for further information. It is my firm impression that they have assisted materially in achieving the purpose which I have described. The statements were completely in accordance with the administrative directive which has been sent to all departments and agencies.
The motion before the house is that an order of the house do issue for a copy of all government statements and directives to government departments during the past year regarding security procedures and investigations. There has been only one such directive, Mr. Speaker, and after the most careful consideration the government has decided that it must, in the public interest, decline to accept the motion to provide a copy of the directive. The hope was expressed that, for this reason, the hon. member might be prepared to withdraw his motion. However, as was his right, he has not seen fit to do so.
Motions for Papers
In declining to accept this motion, the government has taken into account and essentially agrees with the stand taken on this matter by every Canadian government which has had to face this difficult problem. It is essentially this: To divulge publicly the means by which the government instructs its agencies to counter the efforts of those who would steal our vital national secrets and subvert our institutions, would have the effect of impairing the effectiveness of these counter measures. As it was very aptly put in the white paper presented to the parliament of the United Kingdom by the secretary of state for foreign affairs in 1955:
Espionage is carried out in secret. Counterespionage equally depends for its success upon the maximum secrecy of its methods. Nor is it desirable at any moment to let the other side know how much has been discovered or guess at what means have been used to discover it. Nor should they be allowed to know all the steps that have been taken to improve security. These considerations still apply and must be the basic criterion of judging what should or should not be published.
From our experience, and I am sure the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) from the experience he has had will agree, there is no reason now to change the view that has always been taken in this respect. As one of my predecessors in office, Hon. Davie Fulton, minister of justice in the previous administration said on April 29, 1959, as reported on page 3152 of Hansard:
The government has consistently followed the policy of complete reticence concerning security work-
The government which preceded that of which Mr. Fulton was a member also consistently upheld this principle. The present government has gone further in modifying the principle in the interests of supplying information on security matters than any previous government. We fully recognize that it is the government and no other body or individual which has the heavy and undeniable responsibility of advising and administering security policies and procedures which have been agreed upon after years of study based upon our Canadian experience and the collective experience of our allies. We are convinced that to open these detailed procedures to public debate further than has already been done would seriously reduce the effectiveness of these procedures and would lead inevitably to the injury of individuals who have committed no offence under the law. We cannot believe that either of these results would be in the public interest.

Motions for Papers
This is in no sense, Mr. Speaker, a partisan matter. I am sure that hon. members on all sides of the house would be deeply relieved if we did not have to deal with these harsh, complex and difficult matters. But deal with them we must, and in a manner which, based on the best possible knowledge of the circumstances, will afford the best possible protection to the people of this country. In this connection I would ask that hon. members do not underestimate the weight of the responsibility that rests upon the Prime Minister in facing these problems. Indeed I was deeply gratified to hear the right hon. Leader of the Opposition express his recognition of this fact when he said on October 25 last:
Mr. Chairman, the matter under discussion is one of the most difficult problems that faces a government today. It is understandable why the Prime Minister should have made a statement this evening as to the policy of the government, for the responsibility of national security rests primarily on the Prime Minister.
A little later, he went on to say:
From time to time these matters are brought before the people. He carries in his head information in respect to the subject of security that he is almost frightened at times of revealing. The Prime Minister has spoken of the difficulties.
How are you going to maintain security while at the same time preserving and maintaining the fundamental rights of the individual? It is a difficult problem. It is so easy to criticize, but it is so much more difficult, having that responsibility, being desirous of maintaining those freedoms, to be able to carry out one's wishes. Loyalty is expected of all Canadians. It is imperative as a quality of public service.
The maintenance of security is of prime importance to the survival of the state. How often do cases come before a prime minister and he cannot go into the details in the House of Commons? You have the evidence. Often it is secondary evidence; sometimes it is hearsay. The accumulation of hearsay placed before one has an effect, no matter how one endeavours to adopt a judicial attitude.
At the conclusion of his speech, the right hon. gentleman said:
I know the weight of the responsibility that is on the Prime Minister in matters like this-this matter above all. He cannot put it off on somebody else. He in his person has the custody of our survival and our security. In the views he had placed before the house he has been given the benefit of the study that was made by dedicated public servants whose purpose was to assure that justice shall be done. Fiat justitia ruat coelum- 'Let justice be done though the heavens should fall'.
The responsibility is, indeed, a heavy one and not a pleasant one. I am sure it would have given the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) great relief when he was prime minister to have been able to be open and public about all of these things. It is contrary

to the principles on which our society and nation is based to have to maintain secrecy about actions that can, at times, affect the careers of individuals. Yet it is essentially for the protection of our nation, based on those principles, that these measures regretfully have to be taken. Other free nations are faced with the same unpleasant facts of life and recognize that the strong light of publicity cannot be admitted to every detail of security precautions if they are to be effective. It is for this reason that the Prime Minister and the government had to take the position that it would not be in the public interest to publish the current directive on security in the public service. I can however assure hon. members that the new and improved measures to protect the rights of individuals, as described in this house on October 25, are covered in the directive and are in effect.

had thought at the last session of parliament that we had made some progress in this matter of security investigation, but after listening to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) I am convinced we are right back where we started.
The minister has treated the house to the usual parade of the mystique of security- something so secret, something so mystical that it cannot be disclosed to the uninitiated. He tells us of the great burden of responsibility which, he says, the government alone must bear. I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a democratic country in which the government is responsible to parliament and parliament is responsible to the people. The government has responsibility for conducting these security programs. The minister says this is not a partisan matter, and we agree. We have never suggested it was. This is a matter of human justice; it is a matter of deciding whether or not persons who are labelled as security risks and who, in consequence, are either denied employment or dismissed from employment shall have, first, the right to know what they are accused of and, second, an opportunity to present their cases. That is what we are arguing.
All this talk of the minister about the fact that many of these security questions cannot be opened to the light of day is not in dispute. We know perfectly well that security investigations cannot be carried on in a glass house. We are simply contending that people who are accused and who, as a result of the accusation, made, as in some cases, as the minister himself admits from pure hearsay,

shall have the right to lace those who accuse them, the right to defend themselves and to know with what they are charged.
Instead of facing up to this problem the Minister of Justice trotted out the old slogan "Father knows best". I have been listening to this for a quarter of a century. Ministers of justice say: You must leave it to me; you must trust my good judgment and good sense; I am very busy, so this means trusting the good judgment of the officials of my department or of some other department. As a matter of fact we have brought up case after case to show that neither the ministers of the crown nor their officials are infallible. The Gordon Knott case has already been referred to. A number of other cases came before the house in the last session of parliament. I myself have taken up cases with ministers, cases in which the individuals concerned were either being dismissed or threatened with dismissal upon grounds so flimsy that when the ministers themselves looked into them they discarded them and managed to have the cases cleared up. But supposing no one had brought those cases to the attention of the ministers concerned. Supposing the deputy minister or the head of a branch, acting on the report of a security panel, had dismissed the persons in question or refused to hire them. These individuals would then have suffered a great injustice. I pay tribute to the ministers to this extent:	In many cases when certain
matters have been brought to their attention they rectified the situation and saw to it that justice was done. But the number of cases which come to our attention and which we can discuss with ministers amounts to only a small proportion of the cases which occur.
It is not enough, as the old English slogan says, that justice should be done. Justice must appear to be done. It must be clear, beyond doubt, that injustice is not being done. It must be worked into the warp and woof of our government administration that people cannot be unjustly dismissed or discriminated against on the basis of hearsay evidence, on the basis of malicious gossip or on the basis of mistaken identity-and there has been plenty of that-but that the individuals in question shall know why they are being dismissed and what is the case against them, besides having an opportunity to present their cases and, I think, an opportunity to be represented by counsel while a case is being conducted. This is all we are arguing.
Motions for Papers
Last year, the former minister of justice for a while gave us the "Father knows best" routine, and we were relieved when on October 25 the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made the speech to which the Minister of Justice referred this afternoon. The Prime Minister was very generous in saying this:
Since they were introduced in this country in 1947, the so-called security screening procedures adopted have, on the whole, worked well, though of course, Mr. Chairman, there have been mistakes. But I believe we have for the most part avoided excesses both of over-caution and over-confidence. There are nevertheless admittedly certain flaws in the system and it is to these that the government has been directing its attention recently. It is also to these that members have been addressing questions to the government in the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister admitted there have been mistakes and that the system is not without its weaknesses. So he went on, as reported on page 4044, to say this:
After careful consideration the government has come to the conclusion that the essential advantages of these procedures can be achieved within our system by requiring all departments and agencies of government to do two things which they have not previously been required to do. The first of the new requirements is to inform the person involved when his security or reliability is in doubt and may have to involve his dismissal. Employing departments and agencies will in future be required to tell an employee everything that is possible of the reasons for the doubt, if there is a doubt, and to give him an opportunity to resolve that doubt.
That met the first objection. The individual was going to have a chance to know wherewith he was charged, and was to have an opportunity to present his side of the case to the official of the government under whose direction he came. The Prime Minister went on:
The second new requirement is to ensure that a second look is always taken by a separate body before dismissal is finally decided upon. Once the individual is told of security doubts he will have the opportunity to give his side of the case. The employing agency will consider it, consult the staff of the government security panel, and arrive at a conclusion.
I will not bother reading the rest of it; it simply says that if after making his case in the department, the department still abides by its decision, certain things may be done. Then the Prime Minister went on:
But if it is that his dismissal must be recommended, the individual will be given a second hearing, this time by the deputy minister or head of the agency. If that interview does not resolve the doubts, and if the agency head agrees with the view that dismissal is necessary, the whole case and the relevant information, including anything that the employee himself has submitted, will be submitted to a board of review.

Motions for Papers
That was the second thing we wanted. We wanted a quasi judicial board of review. We did not get a quasi judicial board of review; we got an administrative board of review made up of deputy ministers. We are willing to settle for that as an experiment. Therefore the Prime Minister's speech really said two things: First, a man was going to have a right to know what evidence there was to suggest that he was a security risk, and be given an opportunity to answer the charges; second, he was going to have an opportunity of appeal, first from his immediate superior to the deputy minister and then to a board of review. On page 4045 the Prime Minister said:
I feel confident that the procedures which we are now adopting will assist us in making judgments concerning loyalty and reliability in a manner which will protect individual rights as well as national interests.
The Prime Minister said he was confident that this system he was proposing would work. The Minister of Justice has told us today that the government has gone much further than any other government in setting up these two requirements outlined in the Prime Minister's speech. If the Prime Minister is confident that these two procedures are effective in eliminating any possibility of injustice, and if the Minister of Justice really believes that by these procedures the government has gone much further than any other government, why should the government now refuse to make public the material requested in the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North? All this motion asks for is a copy of all government statements and directives to government departments during the past year regarding security procedures and investigations.
The Minister of Justice says there is only one directive. If this directive contains the two proposals outlined in the Prime Minister's speech of October 25, 1963, why should the government hesitate to make it public? If on the other hand it does not carry out the Prime Minister's commitments, I can understand the government's hesitancy about making it available to the members of this house.
Mr. Speaker, on the basis of this directive members of the public service and the armed services in Canada can be dismissed. These people's jobs depend upon the terms of that directive. It is a basic precept that people have the right to know the law. Individuals have the right to know the terms of a directive which affects their security,
[Mr. Douglas.)
their jobs, their reputation and their future. The minister has not given us any reason at all why this directive should not be made public. He has told us that there are a great many security matters which cannot be discussed fully in public. We agree. We are not asking the minister to make public all the facts about any particular security case; we are merely asking him to table a directive sent out to the departments of government setting forth, we hope, in detail the commitments which the Prime Minister of Canada made to the House of Commons on October 25 last.
I know of no reason whatsoever why we should be denied access to this directive. What possible secret information can there be in it? If this directive follows the speech made by the Prime Minister, it should be saying two things: First, that any person about whom there is some doubt as to his or her security status will have the right to know on what that doubt is based and will have an opportunity to resolve the doubt; and second, that directive, if it follows the Prime Minister's commitments, will say that there shall be available to that individual the right of appeal, so that he can go to the deputy minister and can go finally to a board of review and present his case and seek to remove any doubt upon which his dismissal has been recommended. That is all this directive can contain. What is secret about it? What mysterious formula is contained in the directive that is not to be disclosed to the eyes of poor, ignorant members of parliament?
Mr. Speaker, this is just too ridiculous for words. This is part of the mystique of secrecy that has beclouded security in this country for years. The Prime Minister said, when he wound up his speech last year, that he was confident the procedures he was promising would clear up the situation. The Prime Minister having confidence is not sufficient; this house has to have confidence that the procedures have been established and are rectifying the situation which it was all too clear obtained last year. We have not that confidence; we have not been shown anything that would give us that confidence. If the government wants us to have confidence that they have kept faith with the commitments the Prime Minister made on October 25 last, they will give us a copy of this directive. After all, I presume, this directive has been sent to deputy ministers, maybe to branch heads, and to certain personnel in the armed services. Is there any reason why the House of Commons, the members of

which are concerned about this question, should not see the directive? The minister has not given us any reason at all. We are not asking for confidential information; we are not asking for classified material. We are simply asking for a simple directive sent out to guarantee that the ordinary, basic precepts of justice are being adhered to in so far as the public service of Canada is concerned. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is not too much to request.
I hope the minister will give this some further thought and will come back and give us a frank reason for this directive being denied us. I ask him not to treat us like children and expose us to another talk about the difficulty of security measures and the burden this places upon him. We are not asking him to disclose classified data. We are only asking him for a simple directive, a directive which will either prove to us that the government in good faith has carried out the procedures which it promised this house it would implement, or it will show that the government has welshed on its commitments to parliament and has not instituted those procedures. Until the government discloses such directive we have to draw the conclusion that they have failed to implement the procedures the Prime Minister promised would be implemented when he spoke in the house last October.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just sat down stated two alternatives; one from which he drew a conclusion favourable to the government, and the other unfavourable. The first alternative is that the directive referred to today by the minister contains no more than was outlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in his speech last October; the other alternative is that the directive failed to carry out the procedure referred to.
I think on reflection the hon. member will realize in all intellectual honesty and fairness the existence of a third possibility, namely that the directive in question would contain not only reference to the procedure which was set out in this house on October 25, but would also contain additional confidential material, material which could prejudicially disclose the nature of the security structure itself, which would be very prejudicial to our security system as well as prejudicial to the people of Canada and to this parliament to make public at this time.
Motions for Papers
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.

Could I ask the hon. member whether that is purely hypothetical conjecture, or is he making the statement on behalf of the government that it does contain such material? If so, why did not the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) say so?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would point out to the hon. member that this is what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) has said, and said in his statement a few minutes ago, that there was content in this particular directive which, if disclosed, would be prejudicial to the public interest acting through the security system. I think that is a fair observation to make and one which the hon. member in a spirit of fairness would accept.
The hon. member and before him the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) cited examples which spokesmen for the government in October, and again today, have acknowledged as representing a breakdown in the security system. They referred to the Knott and Petersen cases, and I do not think anyone makes the pretence that there was not a definite failure there. It was to meet that particular failure that the procedure set out on October 25 was invoked. I do not think that anyone in any honesty pretends that there may not be some circumstances, very marginal circumstances, in which it might be possible, even through the screen of the new procedure, for some injustices to be done; but I think we recognize that those particular measures which are now being applied would have caught the examples referred to by the hon. member.
I think it is significant to point out-

Mr. Speaker, might I just ask a question. Did the hon. member say, as I thought I heard him say, that there had been an error in the Petersen case? Second, is the parliamentary secretary saying that the procedures now are such that in a similar case the person concerned would be told what were the difficulties so that he could answer them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I did not say that. What I said was that the hon. member referred to examples; and I was referring particularly to the Knott case when I said that the problem which arose there in my opinion would have been adequately caught by the present procedures. As to the second part of

Motions for Papers
-the hon. member's question, I am not saying that even now it would be possible to do this under all the circumstances. As the hon. member requested before, the actual nature of the complaint in some circumstances was that the security officer responsible be presented for confrontation.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I have never said on any occasion that the actual person making the charge against an employee should be brought forward. What I said, and what I will continue to say, is that the nature of the charge should be told to the person concerned. In the Petersen case, Petersen should have been told that it was because his father-in-law was thought to be a communist that he was discharged from the navy. But in his case he was never told what were the reasons for his discharge. I have never said personally, either today or any other time-

No, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member said-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would point out that I have absolutely no intention of misrepresenting the hon. member's opinion, but I have a genuine belief from having heard him before and having heard him again today that that is what he was calling for, namely the right of confrontation in a proceeding similar to a judicial proceeding. If that is not his intention,

then I thank him for making clear to me what was not obvious before.
What I was saying when I was interrupted was that hon. members have not come forward with any instances in which the procedure set out by the Prime Minister and which is now invoked with regard to security matters has failed. The examples which they brought before this house are examples which arose before this procedure, and I suggest that this is a good indication of the effectiveness of the government's measures at meeting this particular problem.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member for Winnipeg North made reference to the procedure which was established under the defence of Canada regulations. I would suggest to him that there is a very substantial difference between the basic merits being decided under those regulations and the very delicate issues being decided by the particular security tribunal concerned. I would point out that the defence of Canada regulations have been promulgated for the purpose of determining the status of someone in Canada during wartime so as to decide whether or not that person would be entitled to be free in our society. They do not determine whether that person would be entitled to access to restricted government information. I suggest, just as was suggested in the speech on October 25 by the Prime Minister, that you have in connection with these security regulations a much more difficult and subtle problem, the problem of determining in a particular case the reliability of a particular employee. That problem would have arisen in Canada in wartime apart altogether from the requirements of the defence of Canada regulations.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to provisional standing order 39A to inform the house that the question to be raised at ten o'clock this evening is as follows:
The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), shifting of ore from Timmins to North Carolina for processing.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

Mr. Speaker, it is with very close attention and indeed with respect that, the other day, I listened to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when he introduced a project for a national flag-three maple leaves on a white field with two vertical sections-and told us, at the same time, the significance for our country to have a truly national flag.
If, on some occasions, I do not always approve of the economic and especially of the financial policy of the government which, in many respects, I consider as retrograde, because it is not in keeping with the needs of more than three million Canadians who are living in want, it gives me pleasure, on this occasion to offer to the right hon. Prime Minister, my most sincere congratulations for the speech-transcendent on many scores -which he made on that occasion when he asked parliament to adopt the proposed national flag so that Canada may be given an emblem which will create a new patriotic climate in favour of our country a mari usque ad mare, because it will contribute to unite all Canadians, since it is a model or a design free from any foreign figurative symbol, and it will mean at long last that our country has attained its majority, that is the age when our bicultural nation reaches adulthood. By adopting that flag, we will give proof of our national maturity.
It is most amazing to see in this house and even outside some parliamentarians who have not yet cut the umbilical cord binding them to another country and who prefer to stagnate in a state of colonial immaturity. Their fanatic opposition to that flag design, typical of Canada in 1964, indicate that they 20220-315
Canadian Flag
are not true Canadians because even if they live in Canada their mind is elsewhere.
The right hon. Prime Minister, in his speech, said this:
The flags we have used for Canada have already changed as Canada has evolved from colony to self-governing dominion to Independent nation, to a sovereign state respected among the states of the world.
In this evolution, the time has now come for another change by the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag which cannot be mistaken for or confused with the emblem of any other country but Canada.
Those are the words of a prominent Canadian, more logical than those of a certain provincial premier who stated, in the last few days, that as long as he would lead his province, the government would fly the red ensign.
Such a statement, like others almost identical to it, reveal the worst kind of separatists that can be found in Canada. Ordinarily, I am a very accommodating man, but faced with such fanaticism and prejudice, I become uncompromising.
The Prime Minister proved with facts that the three maple leaves have a historical and heraldic importance. But, in my opinion, other reasons dictate the choice of the three maple leaves. At all times in history and ancient times, the figure three has been a good number. The three maple leaves express in fact a historical trilogy which marks the development of Canada: the French administration, the English administration, the Canadian administration.
On the other hand, from the viewpoint of natural resources, three leaves make a perfect trio and would show that Canada is a land of plenty, while one leaf would indicate a still life.
In science, three maple leaves could symbolize a triode, for in this automation age, a three-electrode electronic tube plays a major role in quite a number of electronic apparatus.
In music, the three maple leaves could represent a triplet, or three notes of equal value: French Canadians, English Canadians and new Canadians, all of them having equal rights under a bicultural confederation.
From the viewpoint of Christians, who represent the majority of the Canadian people, the Trinity symbolizes unity and, therefore, it is the most beautiful symbol which could grace the future national flag.
For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I approve of the proposed design unreservedly. Besides, as matters stand at present, this is no time for quibbling over this matter, for if we were to pick out a design to suit every

Canadian Flag
member's taste, we would have to approve of 265 different designs.
In concluding, may I add that having advocated for 25 years the establishment of a Canadian republic and called for the red ensign and the union jack to be set aside and replaced by a distinctive flag, I will vote for the three-leaved flag with great patriotic earnestness.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that it has been years since a more important matter than our flag has been brought before the parliament of Canada. In many quarters of this house it is being treated too lightly. We have a flag in our country that has flown for many years. There may be reasons why we may need a more distinctive one. However, first, it must be shown to me that over 50 per cent of the people in this country desire that. It must be shown to me that there are good reasons for changing our flag.
This afternoon the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) said the young people would like this new design and we should please them. I am glad they like this new design. However, there are many who were brought up to honour the design we have today. I have children, and they were taught to honour the flag that flies over our country today. I am sure there are many other young people throughout this country who have the same feeling as my children. We must remember our young people, but at the same time we must not forget the older generations, our fathers, our mothers and our grandfathers and our grandmothers, who lived under difficulties in the pioneering years to build Canada for the younger generation.
I rise, Mr. Speaker, to support the amendment for a referendum on this flag issue. We heard the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) say she was not in favour of a referendum. I may say there are some referendums of which I am not in favour. As an example, I may cite the one held at the exhibition in Winnipeg last Saturday when the Liberal party held a referendum on the question of a sales tax in Manitoba. This is the type of referendum I do not favour, because as I stood there watching these people who were controlling the referendum, one young fellow said to the fellow worker in the booth, "I voted five times today". The other fellow said, "I voted 14 times". I am not in favour of a referendum under those conditions. I want an honest referendum held
[Mr. Cote (Chicoutimi).1
across this country by means of which the people can speak their minds.
I object, Mr. Speaker, to the way in which this resolution was put before this house and the dictatorial manner in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) refused his party a free vote. He held a hammer over the head of the opposition parties by saying, "You either vote for my design or we have an election". I am not in favour of that design. Before I resume my seat tonight, sir, I shall place evidence upon the record which I am sure should cause the Prime Minister to drop his head in shame. I am sure that every Liberal in this house and throughout the country will drop their heads in shame. I am sure this evidence will give those who are supporting this design something to think about.
This flag resolution, Mr. Speaker, is not the type of legislation which can be introduced in this parliament and amended in the next parliament. This is a moral issue across this country, an emotional issue. Speaking for myself, I may say I represent 58,000 people in this House of Commons. I have been sent here on three different occasions to represent these people, the last time with a majority of nearly 10,000. However, I do not feel I have the right to stand in this house and vote on behalf of the people on such a moral and emotional issue as interfering with our flag.
Some people might ask, how would a referendum work? I brought this up before in the house. I feel, sir, we should have a committee of all parties in this house to pick out three designs to put before the people of Canada. The first design would be the red ensign. No. 2 would be an alteration of the red ensign and No. 3 could be a green maple leaf on a red background. The people of Canada would then have an opportunity to choose No. 1, 2 or 3. By a process of elimination of the third and second choices, we would come to a decisive decision of 51 per cent, and whatever that 51 per cent decided I, as a true Canadian, would be glad to support. We understand that at the exhibition in Winnipeg last week, the New Democratic party held another poll. What was the result of that poll? Fifteen thousand people voted, and 75 per cent of them voted for a referendum on the flag. I wonder why there should be such a hurry about getting this flag. What's the hurry all of a sudden? On May 15 the Prime Minister listed the urgent business before the house and there was no mention of a flag. Then, suddenly, we have a flag resolution on the order paper. It appears as

though the flag resolution is nothing more than camouflage to cover up the mess this government has got itself into. The question of a flag should not be mixed up in politics in this way, or used as a means of covering up the weakness of the administration. We have a great deal of urgent business in front of us and we should set about choosing a flag in a better, more democratic way.
We have been united in this country for 96 years. No issue which has been before us has caused so much disunity across this country from ocean to ocean as this flag resolution we are now considering. It is a burning issue across the country. In my opinion it should be shelved so as to give the people a chance to think the matter over. Then it could be brought back into parliament in a more democratic way.
The main reason for the present confusion over the flag issue is that no one has taken the time to study the red ensign and teach it to our children. Let us look at the history of our Canadian red ensign. I should like to thank the Canadian Legion for much of the information I shall be giving in the course of the next few minutes. The Canadian red ensign has gradually grown up with the dominion until today it is the symbol of Canada's place of importance not only among the great dominions of the commonwealth but also among the nations of the world. By common custom the Canadian red ensign has been recognized as a distinctive Canadian flag, and this position was tacitly acknowledged and confirmed publicly by prime minister Mackenzie King, who in 1945 when welcoming General Crerar to the city, turned to the peace tower where the Canadian red ensign waved, and stated:
And that, general, is another problem which your Canadian army has solved for Canada-the matter of our national flag.
Flags, national anthems, and other expressions of a united country grow out of the true history of a people, and the Canadian red ensign has grown out of Canadian history. Next to the staff, the red ensign has the union jack-the emblem which links together all the Queen's subjects. All the dominions use this jack in their flag, proclaiming themselves to be members of the great family of nations who, standing shoulder to shoulder in the last great struggle, sacrificed themselves to aid the oppressed peoples of the earth and who, by announcing to all the world that they will remain firm in that unity, can do so much to stabilize world affairs in the future, in peace as in war. Are we as Canadians ashamed to 20220-315J
Canadian Flag
be known as a member of this great family? The union jack is a union of crosses of three saints-St. George, the patron saint of chivalry; St. Andrew, one of Christ's apostles who was martyred for his faith; and St. Patrick, a missionary who spread among the Irish the civilization learned in France. It is the union of these three crosses which gives special significance to the red ensign as a national flag for Canada.
It is not generally known that in 1921 the Canadian government especially requested His Majesty King George V to order a new coat of arms for Canada. This coat of arms is in use today, and the design of the shield has been displayed on Canada's flag. The Canadian red ensign is a distinctive flag of Canada. These emblems represent the early pioneers who were instrumental in laying the foundation of this great country-English, Welsh, Scottish, Irish and French-all branches of one great race who, coming together in the land of the maple leaf, built a nation of which all may be proud.
So the shield on the flag, while essentially as "new" as the young nation it represents, has its roots firmly in the past and speaks of the very beginnings of our race. The emblems on the shield date back to very ancient times. The couchant lion came to us from France and was the emblem on the flag of William of Normandy, and ever since 1066 has been incorporated in the heraldry of the British kings. The red lion rampant on the golden field is even more ancient. It was the emblem of the Scottish kings and came to them from ancient Ireland, where it had arrived from the east about 580 B.C. The harp emblem is equally ancient and was taken to Ireland by ancient Greek warriors. The fleur-de-lis of the fourth quarter of the shield is well known as the lily of France and held a proud place in the arms of the British kings from the time of Henry II down to the time of George III proclaiming the French ancestry of the sovereigns from the distaff side of the house. It should be remembered that it was this emblem, not the tricolour, which came with the French settlers into this country long before the tricolour was used in France. What we want in our flag, and what we have in our flag today, are the symbols treasured by the people who built Canada. The Pearson pennant is a pretty trade mark but it does not represent the sources of this great country.
In 1924, the Canadian parliament enacted legislation providing for the use of the Canadian red ensign on any Canadian building

Canadian Flag
abroad. Canadian troops fought proudly under the Canadian red ensign in world war II. The Canadian red ensign was carried by Canadians in Korea, and is carried today by them in Cyprus. All Canadian teams at the Olympic games carry the Canadian red ensign. The Canada Shipping Act states: "The Canadian red ensign is hereby declared to be the proper national colours for all Canadian ships."
Until when?

I hear those trained seals yapping away there. They will have plenty of time to make their speeches when I am through. Until then they can sit down. When I am finished they will be able to make their own speeches.
The establishment of the Canadian red ensign through history, tradition and custom, was formalized on September 5, 1945, when our governor general signed an order in council which stated this:
The red ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly may be flown from buildings owned or occupied by the federal government within or without Canada... and it shall be appropriate to fly the Canadian red ensign within or without Canada wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
It will be noted that the order in council stated quite clearly "a distinctive Canadian flag". Those who say Canada has no distinctive flag are either very careless with the truth or they are ignoring Canadian history.
I should like to put on record a letter which came to me here at the House of Commons. It states:
The enclosed article is both interesting and informative. The red ensign has been authorized as our flag by four governments of Canada during the past 70 years, the latest being by order in council (PC 5888) September 5, 1945.
The statement that our flag is not distinctive is, to say the least, erroneous. There can be no doubt in the minds of the Cypriots, Greeks and Turks, when they see the Van Doos and the red ensign, as to where these troops come from.
In the Olympic games the whole world is represented and when Canada sometimes wins a gold medal everybody knows, when the red ensign is raised to the masthead, that Canada has now a world's championship.
With the continued world wide success of Canada as a country, and the extraordinary individual feats of Canadians under this flag, it might not be amiss to wonder who or what is behind this movement to haul down our flag. We should be on our guard that we as Canadians are not being led up the garden path.
That is signed by "Conn" Smythe of the Maple Leaf Gardens.
Where is "Red" Kelly.

I will just give the trained seals a few minutes for a breather, Mr. Speaker. Since the order in council was signed in 1945, immigrants applying for Canadian citizenship are told by the department of immigration:
The flag used as distinctive of Canada is properly described as the red ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly. The flag consists of a red field, with the union jack in the first quarter next to the staff. The inclusion of the union jack signifies Canada's association with the other members of the British commonwealth of nations.
Outstanding French Canadians such as George Etienne Cartier demonstrated their grasp of British constitutionalism as they helped launch the young Canadian nation. Lafontaine, Lemieux, and Laurier drew upon the foundations of British political ideas. As Lemieux expressed it:
If you ask me why I am a British subject and why I wish to remain one, I reply...that I prize most those institutions that secure me most strongly in our rights and liberties-
Many non-British immigrants have made it clear that they support the retention of a flag symbolizing a history in which they now want to participate. Writing as "a refugee from communist tyranny" Mr. Alex Bloschinsky of London, Ontario, states in the pamphlet: "The Canadian Red Ensign" distributed by the Canadian Legion:
In Canada I have found freedom, law, and justice. I and other non-British migrants realize what we owe to the British institutions-constitutional monarchy, parliamentary government, and the rule of law. These are the great bastions of law, order and freedom.
Carried.

Mr. Speaker, I am now quoting from this pamphlet circulated by the Canadian Legion. While I am speaking on this question of a distinctive Canadian flag, it will not hurt to hold up this pamphlet to show the house the banner that is depicted thereon. Two million men served under the red ensign and 111,000 died for Canada under it. This is no time for us, as Canadian citizens, to be kicking this flag about as we are today. The pamphlet says, further:
It is obvious that members of parliament who neither care about nor understand the great Canadian heritage which the Canadian red ensign symbolizes, or who perhaps will vote whichever way they think will further their political future in their party, cannot safely be left to themselves to make one of the most momentous decisions in Canadian history.
This is not a party political question at all: it is one which concerns the very soul of the nation; it is one upon which every Canadian is entitled to have a say now that the government has insisted

that it is an urgent national question. If Canadians are not prepared to act in defence of the symbols of their heritage today, they are inviting the destruction of the very substance of that heritage tomorrow.
Carried.
Question.

Mr. Speaker, now that the trained seals have again had a little relaxation, I will continue. I would like to put on record an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of June 15 last, written by Mr. Bruce West. It is a very fitting editorial and should be put on the record on this occasion:
Of the hundreds of letters on the flag question which have come to my desk in the past few weeks, a good 90 per cent are from correspondents who solidly support the retention of the red ensign. As I mentioned here before, it is difficult to individually acknowledge each one of these welcome notes or even to deal with many of them in this space. There are some writers who object to the idea of a national referendum being held on the flag issue on the grounds that this is a question which should be dealt with only in parliament by the representatives of the people. Yet, as the curtain rises on the flag debate in Ottawa, we are already being told that the adoption of the proposed maple leaf flag is a foregone conclusion. Under such circumstances, it seems that we who support the use of a referendum on this matter could hardly be blamed for wondering just how free and democratic will be the process by which the red ensign is being abolished as the flag of this country. There are others who say that a referendum might cause serious division and dispute in this nation. Yet, if the many who support the retention of the red ensign are ignored and legislation to provide a new flag is virtually railroaded through parliament, how much unity will such an action promote? Still others say that the whole question of what kind of flag we should have is a silly argument in the first place. I don't happen to believe that it is. I believe that the impatient efforts of many to discard a banner which symbolizes almost a century of our history may be a symptom of something gravely unhealthy in the affairs of Canada. I believe such an action might be one more large step toward the day when, stripped of our ancient background and heritage, we may stand as hardly more than another banana republic against the already powerful magnetic pull of our huge neighbour to the south. I hope I'm wrong. But I can't help feeling it, just the same. I feel that upon the day the red ensign is discarded, some vitally important threads are going to be removed from the already strained fabric of this country.
Now you ought to read the Bible.

It wouldn't hurt you to read the Bible a little bit. The flag issue in its present form is bringing great disunity to this country. French and English people who have lived side by side, who have intermar-
Canadian Flag
ried and intermingled over the last 200 years, are now saying they are being forced to split and take sides against each other on the issue. In western Canada we have many French settlers. Many are in my neighbourhood, and we live together and are good neighbours. These people say to me: "What is wrong down east? What is all this talk about? What is all this dissension about? We came west and were welcomed and are happy". Although the founding races of the country were French and English, Canada today is a country of many races. Other ethnic groups came to this country under our present flag looking for political refuge, and got it. Under our present flag today we have freedom of speech, freedom of religion and freedom of the protection of the law.
You will change all that.

You would like to change it but you have not changed it yet, and there will be a lot of snow on the maple leaf before you do change it. Because of our history our Canadian flag must contain an emblem representing both English and French races. Therefore, if we should change our present flag we must retain the union jack in one corner to represent the English and the fleur-de-lis in the other corner to represent the French, with a large green maple leaf on a red background.
Now I come to the important point of my argument tonight. We have heard the argument that we need a new flag because our present flag is too easily mistaken for the British merchant flag; the Prime Minister and others have used that argument. I should like to turn to page 4319 of Hansard, where the Prime Minister is reported as saying:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that a national flag of the kind described in this resolution, that will be exclusively Canadian-
Remember those words "exclusively Canadian". On the next page the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
-I believe that the time has now come for another change by the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag which cannot be mistaken for or confused with the emblem of any other country but Canada.
Hear, hear.

Hon. members are applauding now but they will not be in a minute. Mr. Speaker, you have heard those remarks. Hon. members opposite are concerned because the red ensign may be confused with the British merchant navy flag. I should like to
4SS8

Canadian Flag
refer to "Flags of the World" by H. Gresham Carr which I obtained from the parliamentary library. On turning to page 190 reference is made to the flags of the Soviet union. There appear to be a lot of flags in the U.S.S.R., and this is what is said about the merchant flag of the U.S.S.R.:
The ensign is white, and has a light blue border one sixth the depth of the hoist along the bottom of the flag. In the white portion are the star and crossed hammer and sickle in red-
I suggest that this proposed flag of the Prime Minister is not distinctive from any other flag. We want to destroy our red ensign because it is the symbol of the British merchant marine and replace it with a flag with the white background, the blue trim and the red of the Soviet union.
Shame.
This is a serious matter which should be considered.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order.
I should like to point out to the house that the hon. member has had the floor for 33 minutes. I interrupted only to point out to the Chair that the time of the hon. member should be checked.
