Mr. Speaker, I remember when the former minister of agriculture was speaking in this debate and said that we know what we get when we cross a jackass and a horse. We have just heard them braying. Before I was interrupted I was drawing the attention of the house to the colours of the proposed new flag and its similarity with the Russian merchant marine flag, which has a white background, a blue border and the red

emblem of the Soviet union in the centre of the white. I wonder why the Prime Minister wants to destroy our present flag and force on the people of Canada this design with colours the same as those used by Soviet union merchant vessels. This creates some doubt as to the judgment of the Prime Minister and his advisers and should make the blood of every true Canadian boil. This should give every young Canadian who is supporting this new flag concern for deep thought.
Mr. Speaker, the situation is even more serious now, and in view of what is taking place today I say with all sincerity that there are only two alternatives for the Prime Minister. One is to put this flag issue before the people of Canada by way of a referendum; or else he should resign.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my modest contribution to that of the numerous speakers who have already taken part in this debate. But I shall be very brief, for it is urgent that our country should have its own flag.
In my humble opinion, there is no point in delaying the passing of the measure now before us by asking for a referendum, indulging in obstruction or suggesting that other bills should have priority, because the people want a flag and find ridiculous the objections put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the way he is wasting the time of the house by trying to delay the vote on this resolution.
Could it be that the Leader of the Opposition is afraid of the way some members of his party will vote, especially those from Quebec? Or is he conscience-stricken because he never did bring that measure before the house, despite the huge number of 208 members he had in his group then, when it would have been so much easier for him to give our country the flag for which it has been yearning for so many decades?
Our country needs this emblem to strengthen its national unity and to prove its sovereignty once and for all to the whole world.
As far as the referendum is concerned, I must say to the mover of this amendment that he missed his finest opportunity to conduct a public survey early in 1961 when he was prime minister. Allow me to quote from La Voix de I'Est:
Mr. Diefenbaker has tried lately to advocate a referendum on the flag and the national anthem

issue. He reproaches the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester Pearson, with introducing a resolution in the house on the subject and he maintains that only a referendum could reflect the views of the Canadian people on the selection of a flag and an anthem.
Is Mr. Diefenbaker sincere? Let us ask ourselves, first of all, if he held such a referendum during the six years his government was in office. The answer is no. Mr. Diefenbaker did not hold a referendum on the flag or the national anthem.
You can be sure that if he did not think about it, somebody made the suggestion to him in 1981.
Seeing that the Conservative government had been in office since 1957 and that no decision was apparently being taken in regard to a distinctive flag and a national anthem, a Liberal member placed a bill on the order paper of the house on January 24, 1961.
The bill was tabled on that day by the member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville, Mr. Yvon Dupuis. It was Bill No. 60, "to amend the Statistics Act".
Mr. Diefenbaker had in that bill everything needed to hold a referendum which would not have cost the government anything and would have revealed what the people thought about giving our country a distinctive national flag.
Mr. Diefenbaker had in the house the largest majority ever and there was a proposal he could easily have implemented himself while he was in office, which he is blaming Mr. Pearson today for not doing.
There we are. In 1961, an hon. member pointed out to Prime Minister Diefenbaker and his government how easy it would be to hold such a referendum at the time of the national decennial census, and that project which would have cost the country nothing and would have established the Right Hon. Diefenbaker in the people's mind was discarded.
We must therefore conclude that the present Leader of the Opposition was guilty of two glaring mistakes when in power.
1.	He did not make any decision on the choice of these symbols.
2.	He refused to ask the opinion of the people on the matter at the most convenient time during the last ten years, i.e. during the national census.
He is therefore unjustified to call for a referendum.
I have noted a very strange thing in the speeches of the members of the opposition, namely that almost no member has dared to say that he was in favour of a referendum.
We, Liberals, have promised the people in 1963 a distinctive national flag. The Prime Minister himself during the election campaign promised that such legislation would be passed within two years.
And, so far as I can see, the Canadian public trust our judgment. Besides, I feel a referendum is useless since, as representatives of the people, we have all received a clear mandate. It is up to us to take our responsibilities. If we fail to do so, the electorate will remember it at the next election and they will say and justly so that those who have tried to turn this important question into a political issue no longer deserve their
Canadian Flag
confidence, and their judgment will be without mercy for those irresponsible members.
Consequently, let us pass this resolution as soon as possible; let us stop this childishness; let us act as responsible politicians and the people will be happy and proud of their elected representatives. The public expect a great deal from us; let us not deceive them. If we do not put an end to this, we will be ridiculed by the people and by the rest of the world and we will have deserved it.
I should like to quote this editorial which appeared in La Tribune of Levis:
The government kept its word; the party now in office had promised in the last federal electoral campaign that if it were elected, it would take the necessary steps to give Canada a truly national flag, which, from sea to sea, would be the symbol of a true country.
From the Atlantic to the Pacific, indeed, but also in foreign countries. For, at the present time, it is not exaggerated to say that there are many people, throughout the world, who think that Canada is purely and simply a British colony. Evidently, the red ensign does not help them to think otherwise. For some years, we have been witnessing the birth of many new nations, especially that of the African countries, and we never heard of any particular problem when it came to selecting a symbolic representation which would be agreed upon and recognized everywhere.
As it seems, that in spite of "last minute" delays, the goal is at last within reach, we should rejoice, while just feeling sorry for some members of the "old guard" who refuse to admit what reason, logic and the example of other nations should impress upon us as an unquestionable fact.
Of course, those people may, for some obscure and hidden reason, have a secret preference for a Canada which would not be free but would have to continue "in vitam aeternam" to solicit from a foreign (though friendly) government the ratification of bills and legislation which concern no one but Canadians.
Traditions are a fine thing, but when, to maintain them, national honour, and, by that very fact, part of everybody's individual honour have to be sacrificed, would it not be better, once for all, to abolish those traditions replacing them by mutual goodwill, a spirit and atmosphere of freedom and total respect for the sovereignty of others?
To act, and even to think otherwise, would be to counter progress, to regress, to go backwards, in brief, to do the opposite of what the peoples of the world and individuals everywhere seek to attain.
In respect to the suggested referendum, the very fact that there have only been two plebiscites in this country's history and, I understand, none at all in the whole history of the United Kingdom, would indicate that such formula is not part of our governmental system.
We have here a symbol around which all Canadians, new and old, Canadians by birth, or naturalized Canadians of every racial

Canadian Flag
origin may rally, and which may be the centre and the core of their loyalty to Canada.
I think therefore that the content of this resolution is daring, logical, wise, and that it deserves the support of the house and of all Canadians.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like now to quote the speech made by the Prime Minister when he introduced this motion in the house:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that a national flag of the kind described in this resolution, that will be exclusively Canadian, will bring us closer together; give us a greater feeling of national identity and unity. Today especially, as Mr. Massey has reminded us, we need faith and confidence in ourselves as Canadians, with pride in Canada, devotion to our country. I believe that the adoption of this resolution will help to produce that result. If I did not deeply and sincerely so believe, I would not be introducing it into this House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, this flag, if it is adopted by this parliament, will stand for one Canada; united, strong independent and equal to her tasks. It will recognize that we cannot be saved or sanctified merely by the valour and devotion of our ancestors. It remains to us in each new generation to do our own duty in changing conditions.
To conclude, I want to tell the house that I will vote against the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition, but I will be very proud to vote for the resolution, because I will be happy to tell my children in later years that in 1964, I voted for this flag which is our pride, because I was not afraid to assume my responsibilities and to act as a true Canadian, a true member of parliament and a true representative of the people.
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the hon. member for Levis?
Is the question in order?
Yes.
The hon. member said that he would vote for the maple leaf flag. I should like to ask him whether he will vote for the union jack.

Mr. Speaker, I think it might be safe to say that students of parliamentary government, and I think all

members of the house are that, generally regard as a sort of bible of the duties and the functions of a member of parliament Mr. Edmund Burke's very famous speech delivered to the electors of Bristol well over a hundred years ago. In this speech he set out what the duties of a member of parliament are, and the reasons that he gave are just as valid today, even with radio, television, increased literacy, the press, magazines and other media of public information, as they were when he first set out his dicta. In his speech, as I am sure many hon. members will recall, he points out the difference between being a delegate of the people in the constituency and being a member of parliament, and I think this is a very important distinction to make.
I have had a number of letters, and I am sure other hon. members have had letters as well, saying that it is the duty of parliament and the members of parliament to make a decision on the flag matter. In most cases when I receive such letters I would most certainly agree because that is what members of parliament are sent here to do. As Burke pointed out in his famous speech, members of parliament are sent to parliament to do a number of things. They are sent to parliament to approve the government spending program, to pass legislation and to bring matters to the attention of the public. A great many people, particularly, I am sorry to say, some of those in the field of public media and communication, seem to have forgotten what the function of parliament is. The purpose of parliament is to discuss matters, not to sit apathetically by and accept without proper discussion any proposition that any government puts forward.
To get back to the question of the duty of a member of parliament and what his function is, Burke pointed out very well that since a member of parliament has at his or her disposal the essential facts on any public issue he or she is in a much better position to make a decision on that matter than most of the constituents. There may be some instances where some of the constituents are very well informed but, speaking in general terms, when a public issue comes up a member of parliament is informed or has the opportunity to be informed on the matter to a greater degree than his or her constituents, and it is for that reason that he or she must make the decision.

In 99.9 per cent of all cases this is undoubtedly true, but like most other things that affect human relations and behaviour there are always exceptions because human beings, thank fortune, are not things of metal or stone or computer machines. They have their idiosyncracies, and the exception when a member of parliament is not in a better position to decide certain matters is when he runs into matters of a deep moral or emotional character such as the question of capital punishment, for example. People have very strong personal views on this matter. Matters such as capital punishment are not matters that can really be made political issues because there are enormous differences of opinion even in any political party on such matters, and since these are moral or emotional issues any individual in the country has just as much right to express his or her view on the matter and can do it just as well and just as sincerely as an elected representative.
In my opinion such is the case in the very unique and unusual situation we have before us today, namely the choice of a national flag. This is not a question where a member of parliament has any additional or better information than any of his constituents. This is a moral and emotional matter, one of deep emotional feeling, and every individual in the country has just as much right as a member of this house to express his or her views, because no special knowledge is required to make a decision. This is a moral and emotional issue, one about which there are very deep feelings, as has been made all too evident in the house to date.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Would he explain to us in what way this issue is a moral matter?

I said moral and emotional. The hon. member for Brantford may not regard it as a moral issue but I have had correspondence indicating that a great many people do. Maybe he does not, but that of course is his business. So far as the flag is concerned, I think the people should be able to express their views on the matter.
It has been pointed out that in the history of this country we have had two plebiscites or referendums. One was on the consumption or non-consumption of alcohol and took place in the last century.

That is a moral issue.

That may have been regarded as a moral issue, as the hon. member for Kootenay East points out. That matter was decided by a referendum. Then there was the question of conscription. I do not think that issue was exactly a suitable one for a referendum or plebiscite, but this again is arguable. My view is a personal one and I point out that in that case the government and the members of the house had knowledge at their disposal which their constituents did not and could not have because of security reasons. In that case, the government was in a better position to make a decision. As all of us know, there were other matters involved in the question of conscription. There were racial matters and other things involved, and for that reason it is arguable that it was probably a good idea to have a referendum.
However, I do not believe the case for a referendum on the matter of conscription during the war is the same as the question of a flag. Apparently some of those who supported a plebiscite on the question of conscription are not at all anxious to extend the same courtesy to people from other parts of Canada who feel equally strongly on this matter of the flag.
What do the people of Canada think about this question of a referendum? One hon. member who spoke a short time ago pointed out that a poll was conducted recently in the city of Winnipeg in which 15,000 people cast ballots. I understand the poll was conducted as a public service by the New Democratic party.
Free.

Free, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) points out. I understand from press reports that 65 per cent of the 15,000 favoured a referendum on the subject of the flag. I requested a daily newspaper in my city to conduct a plebiscite in a small way in my constituency. I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that contrary to some views I have heard expressed privately around here, my constituency is not one with a solid Anglo-Saxon background. There are a large number of ethnic groups, if I may use that word, particularly those of German extraction as well as Belgian, Hungarian, Polish and other extractions. Recently a large number of people from the Netherlands settled in this area and became citizens of this country. These people have told me they favour retention of the red ensign because this was the flag they remembered helping to liberate them from

Canadian Flag
the Germans during the last war. It is lor this reason many of these people favour this flag.
However, the newspaper was kind enough to print a ballot showing a picture of the red ensign and a picture of the flag proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). The people were told to mark an X opposite the one they preferred and send the ballot to their member of parliament. The result was very interesting. I have all the ballots here. Those preferring the red ensign totalled 988, while those preferring the maple leaf design advocated by the Prime Minister totalled 184. The people were not required to sign their ballots, but a good many did. I was interested to note that, strangely enough, the majority of those preferring the maple leaf flag seemed to be of Anglo-Saxon extraction, while a large proportion of those favouring the red ensign were of non-Anglo-Saxon extraction. This is something which surprised me a bit.
Many members here believe that as a result of reading newspapers and letters they know what the people are thinking about in Canada. However, I do not believe any of us really know as much as we think we do. It takes a method such as this to find out what the public really are thinking. In addition to these ballots, of course, I have received about 400 or 500 letters from persons. Making a rough calculation, I think I have received about 1,500 representations on the matter from the centre part of my constituency. This comprises the city of Woodstock and the town of Ingersoll, approximately 34,000 persons. Assuming there was one ballot per household, I think this gives a fair cross-section of public opinion on the matter.
Someone may say, well, we have listened to your speech and you have pointed out that in this case a member of parliament should be the delegate of his constituents. Why would it not be all right then for every member of parliament to conduct a sort of referendum in his own constituency and then he would know the views of these people? A national plebiscite would then not be necessary. This argument might have been very well a short while ago, but this procedure is no longer possible because of the manner in which the issue has been presented. After speaking to a great many people, I would say this, that while there are differences of view about the flag design I found no difference of view about one thing. All these people were very critical of the method used by

the Prime Minister in presenting this matter to parliament.
If the Prime Minister had suggested this design and said, "This is a matter of conscience, this design of the flag, so let members vote as they wish on it", I do not believe many people would have had too much objection to that method at all. It would have been quite agreeable. Instead of that, the Prime Minister said, in effect. "This is the flag I am proposing and if it is not adopted by this house there will be an election, the third one within two years". Nobody in the country, but nobody that I can think of, wants an election. The public certainly do not and I do not believe many hon. members in this house do. The Prime Minister made quite certain that the members of his own party would not dare to withhold their support on the matter, although I think perhaps one or two are not going to support it. Some other groups in the house feel that they must support the Prime Minister's flag, for various reasons, one of them being they realize the public do not want an election.
Another reason that I think the method that has been chosen to deal with this matter is unfortunate is that we hear around the country the new flag being called the "Liberal flag". I cannot think of anything more unfortunate than having a political label attached to a symbol which, at some date, may well become our flag. This is a very unfortunate thing, and I am very sorry to hear this reference being made. I say that very sincerely. However, the situation has been precipitated by the Prime Minister and his advisers as a result of the method used to present this flag to the house.
I do not believe the Prime Minister or anyone else should arrogate to themselves the right to design one of our national symbols and place it before parliament. Then, because of the unusual voting situation in this house at the moment, and because of the fact we have had two elections, he virtually forces it on the house. He says, "My design will be accepted or there will be an election." I do not think it is fair; I do not think it is right. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I am most surprised to find the Prime Minister doing this because he has a great reputation in the field of foreign affairs.
It was because of his ability to make compromises and see different points of view. This way there is no compromise possible. There is no consideration whatever for those who wish to express their views, or who do not agree. They are being trampled on. It

seems to me to be out of character for the Prime Minister to do things like that in this country.
May I be permitted a question?

I have had one question already. Time is getting on, I see. At the conclusion of my remarks the hon. member may ask all the questions he pleases.
I suggest it would have been better if the Prime Minister had formed a committee of members of all parties in this house and the other place and had requested that committee within a set and limited time to recommend a design for a Canadian flag. I remember a judge saying to counsel in court during discussion of a damage action settlement, "Have you two gentlemen reached a mutually satisfactory agreement on the amount of damage?" One counsel replied, "Mutually unsatisfactory, my Lord". I imagine if a committee were formed and told they had to make a recommendation within a certain time probably the decision would be mutually unsatisfactory but there would not be just one point of view; at least there would be a compromise of viewpoints in the design.
There are many of us who feel strongly that something in this flag should represent our traditions and institutions. I of course mean that the union jack should form part of our flag. It forms part of the New Zealand flag, part of the Australian flag, and part of the flag of the Union of South Africa, and I am sure my friends from Quebec would hardly call the Union of South Africa a British colony. Yet they retain it and do not find it offensive. The state of Hawaii in the United States retains the union jack as part of its flag because of its traditions, and no one would think that the state of Hawaii was a British colony. Other people think there should be no connection with our institutions or tradition in the flag, urging that we should have something new, regardless of whether it is good or not. I agree, having heard the speech of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) and of the Prime Minister that there is some connection in some of our traditions about the three maple leaves. That we know. But to most people those three leaves do not mean very much; they have to dig around in history books to find where they came from, and I am sure most of us in this house when we learned their origin from the hon. member for Leeds and the Prime Minister were rather surprised to find this out, though I agree it is quite accurate.

We have heard many speeches saying that the flag of Canada should be a distinctive flag and I quite agree. Again we run into ai little problem of semantics. Distinctive means one thing to one person and another to another. Certainly to my friends in the province of Quebec, distinctive means one thing-anything as long as it has not got a union jack in it. To people in other parts of the country distinctive means a flag of unique design which cannot easily be confused with another flag, not even with the Russian merchant marine flag as was pointed out a few moments ago. In that regard I am not at all convinced that there is a strong opposition to the use of the union jack in the province of Quebec as has been pointed out. You may ask what I know about the province of Quebec. I do not know much about it, except that last March I made a speech in this house on the subject of a flag, long before this debate started, and I took the liberty of submitting to the house a proposed modification of the red ensign which I considered might be suitable as a compromise. It was a white ensign with a green maple leaf on the fly and three fleur-de-lis, because I felt strongly that not only the union jack should be retained as representative of our institutions but also that some symbol representing French Canada must be on the flag because, after all, it was the settlers from France who really started this country in the first place and I certainly feel some equally strong representation should be on the flag we have. I feel very strongly and sincerely about that.
In any event the flag was drawn up. A design was made by the Montreal Star and it was published on the front page of the second section. I received a great many letters from people living in the province of Quebec, a good many of them in French which, while I do not speak it very well, I can read as well as English. Much to my surprise the only objections I had then to the flag design were from ultra old school tie Anglo-Saxons.
I did not have any objections from French speaking Canadians. All the letters I received from Quebec on this matter were favourable, stating it was a good design and a good compromise. I am not at all sure that a number of members are not being influenced by a minority view in the province of Quebec. It is true that since the Montreal Star is an English newspaper perhaps a number of people would not have read it, but apparently the Montreal Star has some circulation in

Canadian Flag
the French speaking parts of Montreal because as I have said quite a number of my letters were written to me in French.
The next question, and this is perhaps the biggest question of all concerning the flag is, why now? Why is this matter being placed before parliament at this time and why do they tell us we shall have no chance to get back to our constituencies and find out what our constituents' problems are until this measure has been passed. I have heard it said by members of the Liberal party that this is one of their election promises and they are only carrying it out. That is true, but I do not think it was one of the principal promises made during the election campaign. As far as that goes there were a great many other promises made by the Liberal party in the last election which have been completely broken but which are far more important. I refer to the Canada development fund. And how about those students' free bursaries which were going to be given away? That has been watered down and changed to something else, like a good many other things about which I do not intend to take the time of the house at the present time. I say these other promises are not being kept and are being forgotten, promises as important as this one. Yet there has been no adequate explanation of why this must be dealt with at this time.
In any event the Prime Minister in his election promises said there would be a flag within two years. Well it is just a little over a year. There is plenty of time to appoint a committee of all parties in this house to arrive at a design, or a committee composed of representatives of each province which would probably be equally acceptable, equally good. There would be plenty of time to have a plebiscite on the matter to allow the people to express their viewpoints-lots of time, and still be within his election promise of two years. There is no reason at all why this should not be done. Then, as has been pointed out many times, only last month the Prime Minister told us of the urgent business which must be completed before any summer recess. In the first instance the flag was never mentioned, and then it was suddenly there. Why this indecent haste? Because there has been no adequate explanation from the government a great many people are beginning to wonder. Throughout the country, certainly the parts of the country in which I travel around, one hears this: Oh well, it is pressure from Quebec which has forced the government to bring this issue on. That is one

thing being said. It is also suggested that it is a cynical attempt by the heads of the Liberal party to try to get votes in Quebec, because they are going to have an election fairly soon. That is being said. Then there is another thing that is being said-that it is a quid pro quo obtained by Mr. Lesage and Mr. Levesque for agreeing to the constitutional amendment to bring in the Canada pension plan.
These are the things that are being said. If the government does not know it, it is high time they found out; because I can think of nothing more divisive to this country than the type of talk that is going on. And the reason for it is that no explanation has been given to this house or to the people of Canada as to why this particular design must be forced through-and I repeat this-1 in such indecent haste. There is no reason for it.
We talk about the flag becoming a symbol of national unity; that is what the last speaker, the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) said. It is becoming-and in fact has become already-a symbol of national disunity, because there has been no explanation in this regard. When people do not have explanations, they begin surmising; and what the people of Canada are surmising are those things I have mentioned. Nothing could be more destructive of our country than this. I sincerely dislike hearing things like this, because for years we may have to live with the dissension created by this particular matter. This morning the Globe and Mail in an editorial pointed out that the representation bill, which will re-allocate the federal constituencies, is a most important thing and asked why it is being shelved and put away. We do not hear any more about that particular measure.
Don't tell me that you don't know the answer.

I know that my hon. friend will say that the opposition has filibustered. I have heard it said that this is what the opposition are doing. This did not seem to worry the Prime Minister over the flag, but apparently it did worry him over the redistribution bill, which is something very much more important. This debate is engendering a great deal of bitterness all over the country, which is most unfortunate. To be perfectly fair, I do not think the Prime Minister intended this to happen; I do not believe for a moment that he did. But he has received some awfully bad advice from some of his advisers,

who should have been able to foresee what would happen. This question is now turning into a regular donnybrook all across the country, and it is not helped by some of the remarks that have been made in this house. In addition, it is not being helped by some of the extremist views expressed on this subject, and letters sent to the newspapers.
It certainly has not been helped by a couple of things that have been said recently in what I have always considered to be a reputable and responsible newspaper. I refer to the Ottawa Citizen. First of all there was that shocking cartoon libelling all the exservicemen in Canada, and then only last Tuesday they printed another editorial calling everybody a vigilante who dared stand up in this house and make any remarks that were not favourable to the Prime Minister's flag design. The implication of "vigilante" is that one is a lawless thug, and when a newspaper such as the Ottawa Citizen refers to members of this house, by implication, as lawless thugs because they dare to get up and express the views of their constituents, it is a very shocking thing indeed. I would hope that this newspaper would reconsider its remarks very carefully. It has been said that a plebiscite on the matter of the flag would divide the country. That is all I have ever heard said. Nobody ever said why. This has been done already. Most of the people I have talked to who are in favour of the red ensign have said, "We would be perfectly content, if a plebiscite were held, to accept the results of it; but we do not like the way this thing is being forced down our throats by the Prime Minister and his party. If there were a plebiscite taken, regardless of the result we would accept it." I am quite certain that the people of Canada would do that.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say this. I have already said that I think the Prime Minister was badly advised when he decided to bring this matter before parliament at the present time. It has already created great disunity, great bitterness in this country; and it will create more. I do not think anyone would criticize the Prime Minister at all if he changed his course of action and withdrew his flag resolution at this time and chose one of the many courses of action that have been proposed by members of this house. It has been suggested that this matter be referred to a parliamentary committee. Others have suggested that it be referred to a committee of the provinces, putting a time limit on it so that no one could say it was being stalled. A number of suggestions have
Canadian Flag
been made. It is not for me to say which is the best one, but I do not think anyone would blame the Prime Minister if he took one of these courses of action.
I have heard some of my Liberal friends say, "If we did that, we would be accused of retreat". Well, the Prime Minister has retreated on a good many other things, and I think he would have some very good reason to change his viewpoint on this matter. I do not think anybody would criticize the Prime Minister if he said, "Because of the great row that has been stirred up in Canada, quite unexpectedly, over this flag issue, I would like to reconsider the matter, refer it to a committee and see if we cannot arrive at some kind of compromise design for the flag". A design could be arrived at that all members could support, and would support. Then the government could get out and sell it, and after a period of six months a plebiscite could be held to see whether the people of Canada were prepared to accept the new design. I think the people would accept a new design if this course of action were followed. The thing which people resent is that only a minority of this house and a minority of the representatives of the people of Canada, those who support the Liberal party, have had any say in this matter. I rather gather, from what I have heard, that very few people of the Liberal party had any say in the designing of this flag, either.
Or even support it.

I think the thing that really bothers people is that they have not had any chance to express their view or have any say as to what they consider should be the design of this flag. All of us want a distinctive flag, but it is the method that has been used to go about it that has chiefly concerned the people of this country. I would appeal to the government to change their present course of action and try to work out a design that is acceptable to everybody. They should consult with all the members of this house on this question. Surely the members of the Conservative party, the New Democratic party, the Social Credit party and the Creditistes have as much right to express their views as to what our design should be as has the Prime Minister or the Liberal party. Surely it is to be our flag, and we should have some right to express ourselves. But no; the position the government takes is this, "You can talk all you like, but we are not going to pay any attention to what you say". That is the attitude that is adopted. Therefore I can truthfully

Canadian Flag
say that I think everybody is very justified in resenting this method of approaching the problem.
I would certainly hope the government would decide to change its course of action and let the rest of us in Canada, who are just as good Canadians as those who sit on the government benches, have some say in the choice of our flag.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
Was the red ensign, which the hon. member and many of his colleagues favour and want to retain as the national flag of Canada, chosen by a referendum or a plebiscite?
As I recall, Mr. Speaker, it was chosen by a Liberal prime minister of Canada, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member reconcile, for the benefit of the members of the house, a statement that appeared in his column of May 30 in the Sentinel-Review, in which he stated that his personal choice for a Canadian flag is the red ensign, with the speech he made on March 2 of this session, as reported at page 443 of Hansafd, in which he said:
Is the red ensign a distinctive flag? In some ways you could say it is, but outside of Canada it has been my experience, Mr. Speaker, that despite the coat of arms on the fly the red ensign of Canada is confused with the merchant marine flag of the British navy; to foreigners it looks very much like the old "red duster" of the British merchant marine; and in some cases it is even confused with the Bermudian flag.
How does he, speaking earlier in March for a distinctive flag, reconcile that with his comments on May 30?

Very simply. I still prefer the retention of the red ensign. I agree that in some ways it is sometimes confused abroad. I would favour, as I have already said, making some modification to make it more distinctive, but I prefer the red ensign, and infinitely prefer it to the present design proposed by the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pride that I take my turn in this debate following many of my honourable colleagues in discussing what I feel is one of tMr. Nesbitt.]
the major issues and events of this century. In doing so, like a few others I wish to be brief on the subject. Above all I will endeavour to indicate throughout my remarks the respect I have for those in the house or elsewhere who do not necessarily share my views on this great Canadian problem.
First of all, I should like to make reference to my file on this matter and indicate to the house that it goes back to the early thirties. However, I should like to refer specifically to matters of more recent date in it which will definitely bear more on this debate.
I believe I can honestly say that approximately 200 personal letters have been received by my office. I must admit I have received a great quantity, 40 or more perhaps, consisting of printed matter and to which I attach less importance, because anyone could print a letter and send a copy to each hon. member or have other people send the same printed letter to all hon. members. Over and above the 200 letters, I have received 50 personal letters enclosing a flag design, which is an indication to me not only that the writers favoured for our country a distinctive Canadian flag but that they also tried to indicate what in their view may distinctively represent the will of our nation and its soul abroad. Obviously these 50 letters are in favour of a distinctive flag. Also amongst the 200 letters I have counted approximately 20 which definitely indicate the wish to retain the red ensign.
As I followed the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) I recalled that last November I had the good fortune to represent the Canadian government at the commonwealth conference in Malaysia. At the opening of the lovely parliament buildings there I had to notice the flags flying in front of these new parliament buildings, and like every other member of the delegation 1 looked at these flags flying at a distance because their arrangement did not permit closer examination. I recall that I indicated to some member from another nation which of the flags was the Canadian flag. At that time I presumed that the red ensign was being used for that purpose. A few days after the conference opened I was told by one of the personnel in charge of the bands and other matters of that nature that the flag to which I had pointed on a few occasions as being the Canadian flag was in fact the flag of Bermuda. As we all know, Bermuda is a colony of England, and one of my good friends at the conference, Colonel Tucker, who was the Bermudian representative, indicated to me that they are very well

satisfied to remain a colony of Great Britain. This just helps hon. members to realize the importance of having a flag which would be truly Canadian and distinctive as such.
1 should like to pay tribute to many people in this nation who have helped this parliament to bring about the discussion now taking place to provide a distinctive national flag for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to extend well-deserved congratulations to the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay), my colleague on this side of the house who spoke before me, for his very wise remarks.
I would like also to congratulate the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote) who, speaking for the Social Credit party, expressed so well a little earlier his views on the distinctive flag proposed for our country and his decision to support it.

I think we owe thanks to many groups in Canada for the many years work they have done to make sure that the Canadian people and the representatives of the people realize from decade to decade the importance of adopting a distinctive national flag. I am sure hon. members will appreciate it if I make special reference to the Native Sons of Canada. I carried on correspondence with this association in the early thirties and they are the type of group which have presented their views on this matter. I should also like to make reference to the league for a Canadian flag of the province of Quebec, which has done great work in making sure that all people who want to be informed on the values and significance of flags should be so informed.
It has been said that the proposed flag would either bring about unity or disunity. I am one of those who feel certain that Canada can be united, and in a way which would be permanent, by the adoption of a distinctive flag, which would mean that every Canadian from sea to sea could point to the insignia which would be the flag of Canada and could say: "This represents me. I am a Canadian".
I should like to recall the words used a moment ago by the hon. member for Oxford, who apparently found occasion to indicate the wishes of the Anglo-Saxons, the French, and others. I feel all Canadians could find in a national flag, a flag which is distinctive, a flag which is unique, a flag which caters to
Canadian Flag
no one in particular, something whereby they could unite.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right; it means nothing.

I respect and appreciate the view that we should adopt the red ensign because certain people feel it should be retained. I admit the sentiments behind this. I appreciate and respect them; but surely it is a different matter when the government offers an emblem to every Canadian, an emblem which can represent each and every one on equal terms.
I know there are people who will say, "Accept this one; it is most favourable to us. It may not necessarily appeal to you but please conform to our wishes." While I respect their wishes I believe that something which is not Anglo-Saxon or French, and that does not pertain to any other national group, should be used to unite our people. In bringing this proposal before the house I trust no one will blame the Prime Minister by trying to indicate that those who favour a truly distinctive Canadian flag are disloyal to allies from whom we have received so much and whom we respect. That should not be the case.
I recall being invited to speak to a branch of the Canadian Legion in my riding, and I told the members I would indicate to this house what happened at the end of the meeting. The president of the meeting requested a standing vote on the red ensign and the great majority of the members present, some 75 or 80, stood up in favour of the ensign. But I must also tell the house that some members did not stand. I also recall speaking to a meeting at the Carl Nesbitt school in my riding, and these were but two instances during recent times when I was invited to speak on the flag question. At that second meeting somebody indicated that it was disloyal to, shall we say, put aside the red ensign, and I had occasion to tell the group an incident which took place some years ago when a gentleman came into my law office seeking advice.
He was what we sometimes refer to as a new Canadian and he was asking me how to go about changing his name. His name was Sienkiewicz, I recalled that was the name of the author of "Quo Vadis", a book which I enjoyed reading very much. I asked him if he were related to the author and he told me his family considered they were. He told me of his parents who were still in his motherland and how he would like to see

them here in Canada enjoying the liberty which Canada gives to Canadians. I ask you, was this gentleman pushing aside his family in wanting to change his name? Not at all; I recall he took pictures of his family from his wallet and showed them to me. Notwithstanding his love and affection for those he left behind he was trying to give himself something that would be more suited to the country he was now enjoying. Therefore I say let us not try to play on words, indicating that because we want something which will be truly ours that we are pushing aside others whom we have always respected and will continue to respect.
Some people say that a referendum should be held on the flag issue. The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who preceded me, seemed to be surprised by the fact that the Canadian parliament is discussing a national flag. He seemed to think that this was something which has come about suddenly; but I can tell him that as a Liberal for many years, and more specifically during the last two election campaigns, my program and that of my party has always included a distinctive Canadian flag. In fact I believe that all parties in this house have included a distinctive flag in their election platforms.
I have heard some hon. members especially those on the Conservative side, say that we do not seem to know what a distinctive Canadian flag would really mean. Nevertheless as I have said, it is part of the platform of all parties and it should not be any surprise that parliament is now being asked to decide the question; it should not be surprising that we who begged votes are now being asked to do what we promised to do. It is in the fulfilment of promises that in a democracy such as ours we are able to give the people those things for which democracy stands. Our people know, through the democratic evolvement of our parliaments, that they will obtain a full degree of maturity.
Before closing I should like to say a word or two about an official flag which, according to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, would be the red ensign. I have heard many speeches in this house and elsewhere which would lead one to believe that we do have an official Canadian flag at this time, but I believe the case was very well put by the Prime Minister, on the opening day of this debate, when he indicated exactly where the law stood, and that permission was given in 1944 or 1945 permitting the use of the red ensign until parliament took action. That is what we are now doing in 1964.

Canadian Flag
If it were so, that the order in council really meant granting a distinctive flag for Canada, how could the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, the man who was the author of that order in council, proceed the following year to demand that a committee be established to study the flag which Canada might give itself?
I have had occasion to travel throughout Ontario recently and was asked to speak to the children at the Carl Nesbitt school in my riding. I had been invited to speak on the flag question and I first congratulated the students for their interest in this great national problem. I said I should like to start by asking them this question: Have we an official flag in Canada? A little girl in the front row got up, as did a young lad in about the tenth row. I said, "Yes, young lady", and she said, "No, we do not have an official flag in Canada". I said to the young man, "What is your opinion?" He said, "Mr. Godin, we do have an official flag." I said, "You say we have. Which flag is it?" He said, "The red ensign". Then I said, "We can now start the discussion. I should like to indicate my views to you, and my views are those of the young girl." I told them that I must prove my views just as I must prove them to the house tonight. I said to them, "The best proof I can give you is that as I drove up to the school I looked up at the flagpole and saw the union jack flying there, which we all know is the flag of another nation."
It is in the second resolution.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What are you going to do about the second resolution?

It is out of order to discuss the second resolution now, but I might make this remark. The second resolution does not pertain to the flag of Canada, which is what we are now discussing. We are now considering the resolution which, if passed upon favourably, will grant Canada a distinctive national flag. I have no quarrel with granting respect to the attachment that some people may have for the monarch of Canada and the relationship that has existed between our two countries.
When I told these school children what flag was flying over their school it was in the presence of the members of the school board, the principal of the school and 17 or 18 school teachers. I said to them, "Young children, surely if we had an official distinctive national flag the school board would not fly the flag of another nation over this school".

That surprised the principal and most of the people there, I am sure. Therefore with regard to the question of one flag being official I think that the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), based on facts, based on the history of the flag situation portray the true picture.
Today in 1964 we are doing precisely what people in 1944 thought we should work toward. I trust that members of this house, accepting their responsibility to represent the people who elected them, will decide this question on the basis of the evidence presented to the house and that Canada will be favoured with a distinctive national flag through which and by which, I am sure, all groups will be able to progress because I believe that in a few years from now all Canadians, no matter what their beliefs are today, will honour the flag chosen by parliament in 1964.

Mr. Speaker, could I direct a question to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) who has just sat down?
I know that he will vote for the flag with three maple leaves but I would like to ask him if he will vote also for the union jack?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion today, July 2, is a very appropriate time to resume the debate on the resolution which would take away our Canadian red ensign and all the history and tradition associated with it. I say that July 2 is a very appropriate day for this flag debate because, of course, it follows immediately after Canada's 97th birthday and the celebrations connected with this long period of very proud history.
From the ruddy glow of health on the faces of many members of the house I judge that they had the same experience I had on July 1, the experience of participating as a spectator in the formal celebrations of Dominion day. It was a well rehearsed Dominion day observance and I congratulate those responsible for the planning and rehearsing. In the years I have been here Dominion day has always had great significance for me in connection with my parliamentary duties and obligations.
This Dominion day of 1964 had particular significance. I am sure this was impressed on all of us in each part of the day's program. There was the changing of the guard, the artillery salute of 21 guns in honour of
Canadian Flag
Dominion day, the carillon recital, the presentation of folk songs and dances by groups representing each of the 10 provinces, martial music by the central band of the Royal Canadian Air Force and then the ceremonies by the armed forces with the royal salute to His Excellency the Governor General.
The ceremony by the armed forces was staged on the front lawn of parliament hill before at least 10,000 people, with 66 Canadian red ensigns, to which some members of the house object, fluttering in the breeze. I am sure this was a sight which must have thrilled all of the 10,000, including the Prime Minister himself. Naturally it was not possible for me to obtain the impression of all those present but I did speak to as many as I could after the celebration and the general reaction was:	Let us keep the flag we
have now.
I mention the Dominion day crowd because the amendment to the resolution before us proposes that we have a plebiscite on the flag issue. If a poll could have been taken of the 10,000 watching the Dominion day ceremony, I am sure the Prime Minister would have been told in no uncertain terms that this most certainly is not the time to try to impose his three maple leaves design on Canadians as a new national flag.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, that we could have held this flag debate out on the lawn in the presence of those 10,000 people as part of the Dominion day observance. If this were possible, I am sure we could have shown clearly to them the logic of the situation as it actually exists in this house, and shown them why we take the stand we do against the three maple leaf design, and why we are calling for a plebiscite to let the Canadian people decide the issue.
I wish all Canadians could be present to hear this debate, then they would not have to read the newspapers or hear over the radio and television the comments of the writers who so often present their personal views as though they were actual fact. I take strong exception, Mr. Speaker, to the biased opinion of one of these commentators who used an entire C.B.C.-T.V. audience to work out some personal spite on opposition members who are presenting the views of their constituents against the three maple leaf design. I will not mention the name of this writer, commentator, editor or whatever he wishes to call himself because I know he dearly loves publicity. However, I will mention that "Bark" is part of his name and that is what he did during most of his comments. The whole theme of his

Canadian Flag
comments was a defence of the Prime Minister's ultimatum that we must forget our responsibilities in parliament and allow the Canadian red ensign to be removed without further argument.
This "barking" commentator, of course, is a friend of the government. You have here a double-barreled ultimatum to the opposition. On the one hand, the Prime Minister says, pass my flag design now or there will be no summer recess, and on the other hand this commentator friend says, the opposition members who are presenting their constituents' views are, and these are his words, pettifogging politicians, trouble makers and irresponsible members who are holding parliament up to public contempt. I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that my indignation at the biased and unfair remarks of the television commentator have taken me from my reference to Dominion day.
Each item on the July 1 program had a history and a tradition behind it, as symbolized by the 66 Canadian red ensigns waving so proudly. It is this Dominion day tradition behind the red ensign that we are emphasizing in this debate. This tradition can be expressed in no better words than those appearing in the last issue of the United Church Observer. I quote:
A hoop rolls on only if given a regular tap. Just so the stories of a nation travel down the years if occasionally touched upon. July first is a good time to brush off the dust and bring to light the story of the naming of Canada and also the story of the word "Dominion".
This is the quotation from the United Church Observer to which I should like to call the attention of the house. There is also a great tradition behind Dominion day. Last Wednesday in this house the Prime Minister stated, as reported in Hansard for June 24, at page 4651:
This attachment to tradition is an important element in a country that wishes progress.
In this flag debate the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) said, as reported in Hansard for June 30, at page 4912, that we must retain those things of our past for which we have so much genuine affection and loyalty. Where is all this history and tradition in the proposed three maple leaf design? The member for Leeds (Mr. Mathe-son), as reported on page 4884 of Hansard for June 30, asked, what is better than this long established sprig of sugar maple to portray us to ourselves and to the world? Then, he commented on what he called, the flag about to be born, about to flutter on our

plains and on our mountains. I come from the plains, the plains of Saskatchewan, where there are no sugar maple trees, no tradition regarding such a tree or the maple leaves on it.
In this connection, if I may, I should like to quote briefly from an article written by Patrick Nicholson on February 23, 1960 when he was concerned about this flag question. I quote:
Many would build the flag around the maple leaf, the adoption of which would make us appear as a colony of the state of Vermont, or perhaps of Rhode Island or Wisconsin, which have already adopted the maple leaf as their symbol.
Apparently some areas in our country have a greater maple leaf tradition than we have on the prairies, and the proposed three maple leaf design might have more appeal there. I was surprised, Mr. Speaker, to hear the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) say that we are here in parliament to make decisions regardless of what our constituents want. I do not subscribe to this view. I want to put on the record some of the views of my constituents, views that I personally support, but even if I did not I would feel obliged, as the representative of these people, to express them in parliament. I ask members opposite to do the same. I am sure many of them have received letters supporting the Canadian red ensign. I have three full files of letters from constituents on the flag issue. I have not the time in this debate to read them all, but I want to place representative comments on the record. I shall just take pertinent comments from several of these letters. This one is from Stony Beach in my area:
Everyone we contacted and that really Included the five school districts and outside districts as well were 100 per cent in favour of the red ensign. Even the staunchest Liberal supporters were in favour of the red ensign. We have approximately 90 families in Stony Beach area and contacted them at school field days, 4H achievement days, sales and meetings.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, this was a fairly good canvass of that area. Here is a letter from a farmer now living in Moose Jaw:
We have a distinctive flag in the red ensign. Let them add a large maple leaf if they wish but let's not toss it aside. Most of the people of Moose Jaw feel this way and we hope you can help us express our wishes.
This letter is from Regina and concludes as follows:
Therefore I ask that you consider voting against the proposed maple leaf ensign, and exert influence

where possible to have an amendment proposed designating the red ensign as our flag.
This letter is from my own city of Moose Jaw, and reads in part as follows:
I do believe the flag issue has caused a disquieting feeling among a number of people, for they express an opinion that there are more pressing things by way of problems in Canada that parliament should be dealing with, and the flag issue should be set aside for the time being and these more pressing problems dealt with.
There we have an expression of opinion about the problems of this country.
This letter is from Lumsden, Saskatchewan, and reads in part as follows:
Seeing that this country was won for the British Empire under the union jack, and seeing also that Canadians fought under the red ensign (which of course incorporates the union jack) in two world wars, and further as I myself am a veteran of both world wars I could not accept or respect any flag for Canada which did not incorporate the union jack in its design.
Here is a letter from Semans, in my area, and this has a direct bearing on the question of the plebiscite.
As for the people around here, whether they are for the red ensign or not, the vast majority feel that a new flag should not be imposed on us without a national referendum. They feel that if the majority of the Canadian people want a new flag then a new flag it should be, but if the majority want the red ensign then the red ensign should be maintained.
Just a line from Craven:
Our old flag, the red ensign, will always be my flag, and the majority of the people in this area have the same opinion including a lot of the Prime Minister's own supporters.
Another from Watrous:
Most of the people I have spoken with are in favour of the red ensign and those who are lukewarm on the subject at least feel there should be a vote on the matter.
The next one expresses an opinion of many people in Canada. It refers to the situation in Moose Jaw where it says there are six to one in favour of the red ensign, and adds:
The other one is the Liberals who are so disgusted with the manoeuvring of their party in Ottawa that the flag issue is the only red herring they have left, so they favour the new flag.
I have dozens of these letters and I will take no more time to put them on record. But I did go through the list and I have here a summary. There are 30 of the important towns and districts in my area represented in this file, and they all express the same comment as I have given so far.
Now if I could just turn to the city of Moose Jaw. As I said before, they have had a survey there which I think would be along
Canadian Flag
the lines of what would happen in a plebiscite, and here is the last comment on it in the Times-Herald of June 15, 1964. The heading is: "Flag Decision Settled in City".
Members of parliament today began the battle of the flags in Ottawa, but Times-Herald readers have already decided the controversial issue.
Final results of the Times-Herald flag poll show overwhelming approval for the red ensign... this makes a more than 80 per cent majority on the side of the old flag.
They held a street survey, stopping people and asking them what flag they preferred, and the pictures of the people they asked are shown on another page under the heading "Six to One for the Red Ensign".
So far I have dealt mainly with individual letters I have received. Of course, I also received a large number of letters from organizations, principally from branches of the Canadian Legion in my area. Concern in Moose Jaw is so strong that they have had a petition circulated and I understand the Prime Minister received this signed petition recently asking for the retention of the Canadian red ensign. Then I have letters from various lodges of I.O.D.E. and the ladies Orange benevolent association. There are a number of these; they are all on the same theme, the retention of the Canadian red ensign. There is one from the Royal Canadian Legion Semans branch beginning:
We strongly deplore the arbitrary action of your minority government in dictating to the people that they shall have a new flag. This contravenes the democratic rights of every Canadian. We respectfully urge that the government call a national plebliscite and restore to the people their democratic privilege of deciding whether they want the red ensign or a new flag.
That was sent to the Prime Minister. It adds that copies were being sent to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), to myself, and to the leaders of the other parties in this house. This is accompanied by a petition signed, I would think, by a representative of every family in Semans. They all ask for the retention of the red ensign.
The army, navy and air force veterans in Moose Jaw through their secretary-manager also sent in a statement as follows:
We, 756 members of the army, navy and air force veterans in Canada, Moose Jaw unit No. 252, do petition you for the endorsation of the red ensign as the national flag.
The comrades who answered the roll call for the last time would not have it changed to any other flag and we, the living, shall maintain and uphold their sacred pledge.
This flag represents the Christian way of life, the aristocracy of achievement of the four freedoms.

Then I have received a letter from the sons of England benefit society along the same lines. Also, I have one here from the Royal Canadian Legion in Saskatoon. May I say that I understand the newly elected member for Saskatoon arrived in Ottawa tonight and will probably be in the house tomorrow.
Hear, hear.

This letter from Saskatoon says:
In view of the fact that at present there is no sitting member for the Saskatoon constituency the members of our branch request that you give your consideration to the following resolution:
Resolved that we urge delay in the proposed legislation for the adoption of the new flag and propose retention of the red ensign as Canada's flag until more assurance is obtained that this legislation has the consent of the nation.
That was written before the by-election.
As I say, the newly elected member for Saskatoon will, I imagine, be in the house tomorrow and she will probably take part in this debate. I just wanted to bring this matter to the attention of the house now, and I hope to be able to amplify my remarks later.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it 10.30?

subsubtopic: PROCESSING OF ORE FROM NEW MINING DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
In the seven minutes at my disposal it will be difficult for me to deal in any detail with the subject I wish to raise; I shall only be able to cover it in what might be called skeleton form.
I am raising this matter tonight because of two things. The first is the recent announcement by Texas Gulf that the intention is, until such time as the product of the big copper strike in Timmins gets really rolling, to export the ore to be processed outside this country. My second reason for raising this matter now is a remark overheard by a Timmins businessman who was attending a meeting in New York when this matter was discussed. An executive of Texas Gulf mentioned they would like to ship the ore to North Carolina but they did not know what the people of Timmins would think


about this. And Mr. Jules Timmins who is, I believe, one of the top men in the Hol-linger organization, made the statement that they did not have anything to worry about as far as the people of Timmins were concerned because the business people of Timmins were a bunch of jellyfish and you could walk all over them.
There are only two ways in which this ore can be shipped at the present time. One is by getting an export permit from the government of Ontario, and the second would be by getting a special freight rate over the Ontario Northland railway, which is owned by the people of Ontario, to ship this ore over the great distance contemplated. It might be said that this is a purely provincial matter, but it is not entirely so because the people of Canada as a whole have a great interest in this development. In the first place, the Timmins area has been designated as one of the designated areas of Canada that is in need of attention from the federal government. In fact, a conference was held as recently as June 17 last at which the officials of the Department of Industry explained the benefits that can be obtained under this program. I attended that conference, along with some 80 or 90 businessmen of that area.
To bring to the attention of the house the magnitude of this situation, I would like to point out that in 1926 when Noranda decided to build a smelter they had ore reserves of one million tons. Some 37 years later, in 1963, after being in production for that period of time, they had reserves of some 11 million tons. In Murdochville, Quebec, when they started in 1952 they had ore reserves of some 67 million tons in the three properties there. Today, 11 years after, they have ore reserves of some 55 million tons. With regard to the strike in Timmins, when the diamond drills reached 800 feet they estimated there were some 25 million tons of ore, at 1,400 feet the estimate was 55 million tons. I am now told that the drills are down to the 2,700 foot level and they have hit ore that is the richest deposit yet, and it is broadening out. I was told by a man who works in the field and has prospected for many years that a sensible estimate of this ore is some 300 million tons.
In the June 27 issue of the Financial Post the picture is traced as follows: 55 million tons averaging 4.85 ounces of silver, 1.33 per cent copper and 7.08 per cent zinc. This tonnage is contained in a body 1,800 feet long and 200 to 500 feet wide. One of the 26 holes drilled has probed to 1,400 feet and is still in

ore; and they are now at 2,700 feet and it gets richer as it goes along.
My point is that the jobs which the federal government should be interested in are involved in the smelting and processing of this ore rather than the actual mining of it. If we lose the smelter, all we will have is a great big hole in the ground and the jobs this great find should be providing will be provided in another country rather than our own. The second point is this. If the smelter is not built there will be no opportunity to establish secondary industry such as copper wire production, electronic fixtures and things of this nature. A whole industrial complex could be built around this project. Another thing which the federal government should interest itself in is that of exchange between the United States and Canada. This is a very important aspect of this operation. A smelter must be built for this operation, regardless of where it is built. The smelters of Sudbury and Rouyn-Noranda can possibly handle the copper production, but they cannot handle the zinc. A plant will have to be built for this purpose, and it should be built in this area. Timmins has everything that is required. There is the mighty Mattagami river; there is everything that is needed for industrial purposes. There is power at Abitibi canyon, the Little Long rapids, and everything that is needed for this industry. There is natural gas running through to southern Ontario and thousands and thousands of acres of land that could be bought at a very reasonable price, rather than going into southern Ontario or some other place where you might have tc plow up fruit orchards and things of that sort
Another important point, Mr. Speaker, is that the smelter should be a custom smelter. If Texas Gulf builds a smelter it could only be for their purpose and other operators will have to ship 100 miles or more, which will mean a difference of $5 or $6 a ton in trying to exploit their production. I would suggest that the government-I see that my time is running out, Mr. Speaker-look into this matter and should if necessary offer to build a smelter on their own. I think it would be a wonderful investment in Ontario for this government and would greatly assist the employment situation in the area.
Last, but far from least, action should be taken, and taken now, because once this ore starts to be shipped out the plans will have been made beforehand and it will be too late to turn the clock back.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not exactly sure of the question the hon. member was addressing to the government, but I would observe this, that while the government is eager, especially in the designated area of Timmins, to see the maximum of industrial growth, and at the greatest possible rate, the action the hon. member has recommended or is suggesting seems to lie principally in the hands of the government of Ontario, and it would be inappropriate for me to comment on action or inaction on the part of another government.
The hon. member has drawn to my attention that one of the advantages of Timmins is the availability of large quantities of natural gas in the area. This represents initiative taken by the previous Liberal administration and I hope that we will be successful in the present instance in providing further advantage to Timmins.
